questions.question: The SI unit of pressure is
questions.explanation: Pressure = force/area → N/m² = pascal (Pa). Newton is force, joule is energy, watt is power.

questions.question: The dimensional formula of force is
questions.explanation: F = ma → M × LT⁻² = MLT⁻². Energy is [ML²T⁻²], momentum is [MLT⁻¹] and pressure is [ML⁻¹T⁻²] — keep this set straight.

questions.question: The number of significant figures in 0.00520 m is
questions.explanation: Leading zeros don't count; the trailing zero after a decimal point does. So 5, 2, 0 → 3 significant figures.

questions.question: Which of the following is a dimensionless quantity?
questions.explanation: Strain = change in dimension/original dimension → a pure ratio. Angle, refractive index and relative density are the other standard dimensionless quantities.

questions.question: The dimensional formula of Planck's constant is
questions.explanation: E = hν → h = E/ν = ML²T⁻²/T⁻¹ = ML²T⁻¹, the same as angular momentum. That's why ħ is the natural unit of spin.

questions.question: 1 light year is approximately
questions.explanation: Distance light travels in one year = 3×10⁸ × 3.156×10⁷ ≈ 9.46×10¹⁵ m. The 1.5×10¹¹ m figure is 1 astronomical unit (Earth–Sun distance).

questions.question: The dimensional formula of the coefficient of viscosity is
questions.explanation: From F = ηA(dv/dx): η = (MLT⁻²)/(L²·T⁻¹) = ML⁻¹T⁻¹. Its SI unit is the poiseuille (Pa·s) — and it's the quantity that makes honey flow slowly.

questions.question: For x = at + bt², the dimensions of b are
questions.explanation: Every term of a physical equation must have the same dimensions. So [bt²] = [x] = L → b = L/T² = LT⁻² (it plays the role of ½a).

questions.question: Which pair of quantities has the SAME dimensions?
questions.explanation: Both are ML²T⁻². Torque = r × F and work = F·d look similar dimensionally, but torque is a vector (r ⊥ F) while work is a scalar (dot product) — dimensionally identical yet physically different.

questions.question: The number of base units in the SI system is
questions.explanation: Seven base units: metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela. Everything else (newton, joule, pascal, volt…) is derived from these.

questions.question: The dimensional formula of RC (resistance × capacitance) is
questions.explanation: RC is the time constant of an RC circuit — it has the dimensions of time, T. Checking units before substituting values is the single best habit for electronics numericals.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a unit of energy?
questions.explanation: Watt = joule per second, which is power. Erg (10⁻⁷ J) and kilowatt-hour (3.6 × 10⁶ J) are both energy units, as is the electron-volt.

questions.question: If v = a/(t + b), the dimensions of a and b respectively are
questions.explanation: The denominator must have the same dimensions as t, so b = T. Then a = v × t = (LT⁻¹)(T) = L. Additions must always match dimensions — that's what fixes a and b.

questions.question: The dimensional formula of Stefan's constant (σ), where E = σT⁴ per unit area per unit time, is
questions.explanation: Power per unit area = ML²T⁻³/L² = MT⁻³, and dividing by T⁴ gives MT⁻³K⁻⁴. This makes σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, the Stefan–Boltzmann constant.

questions.question: If E, M, J and G denote energy, mass, angular momentum and gravitational constant, then EJ²/M⁵G² is
options: a quantity with dimensions of time
a quantity with dimensions of length
a quantity with dimensions of power
questions.explanation: EJ² = (ML²T⁻²)(M²L⁴T⁻²) = M³L⁶T⁻⁴ and M⁵G² = M⁵(M⁻²L⁶T⁻⁴) = M³L⁶T⁻⁴. The ratio is dimensionless — you can build dimensional 'recipes' like this only if the exponents cancel exactly.

questions.question: The density of a cube is found by measuring mass with 2% error and the side with 1% error. The maximum percentage error in density is
questions.explanation: ρ = m/a³ → Δρ/ρ = Δm/m + 3(Δa/a) = 2% + 3(1%) = 5%. Powers multiply the error — that's why error answers are always built by counting exponents.

questions.question: The dimensions of angular momentum are
questions.explanation: L = mvr = M × LT⁻¹ × L = ML²T⁻¹, identical to Planck's constant. Note the difference from linear momentum [MLT⁻¹] — an extra L.

questions.question: The dimensional formula of permeability of free space μ₀ is
questions.explanation: From F/l = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd): μ₀ = (MLT⁻²)/(A²) = MLT⁻²A⁻². Its companion ε₀ has [M⁻¹L⁻³T⁴A²], and 1/√(μ₀ε₀) = c — a nice dimensional sanity check.

questions.question: A screw gauge has a pitch of 0.5 mm and 50 divisions on its circular scale. Its least count is
questions.explanation: Least count = pitch/number of circular divisions = 0.5/50 = 0.01 mm. Screw gauges read to 0.01 mm — far finer than a vernier callipers (0.1 mm).

questions.question: g is determined from T = 2π√(L/g). If L has 2% error and T has 1% error, the maximum error in g is
questions.explanation: g = 4π²L/T² → Δg/g = ΔL/L + 2ΔT/T = 2% + 2(1%) = 4%. The factor 2 appears because T is squared — square a quantity and its error doubles.

questions.question: Which of the following is a SYSTEMATIC error?
options: Zero error of a measuring instrument
Change in temperature reading to reading
questions.explanation: Systematic errors have a definite cause and a fixed direction (zero error, wrong calibration, end error) and can be corrected. Random errors scatter both ways and are reduced by averaging.

questions.question: The volume of a sphere is computed from r = (2.00 ± 0.01) cm. The percentage error in the volume is
questions.explanation: V = (4/3)πr³ → ΔV/V = 3 × (0.01/2.00) × 100 = 3 × 0.5% = 1.5%. Only the exponent of r matters — the constant 4π/3 contributes no error.

questions.question: The number of significant figures in 0.0003020 is
questions.explanation: Ignore the leading zeros: 3, 0, 2, 0 → 4 significant figures. The trailing zero after a decimal point is always significant.

questions.question: Dimensional analysis: √(LC) has the same dimensions as
questions.explanation: In an LC circuit ω = 1/√(LC), so √(LC) = 1/ω and has dimensions of time — it's the period of oscillation. Dimensional checks like this catch most formula errors.

questions.question: Which of the following has the same dimensions as impulse?
questions.explanation: Impulse = FΔt = MLT⁻¹, exactly the dimensions of momentum — which is just the impulse–momentum theorem restated. Force is MLT⁻², work is ML²T⁻² and power is ML²T⁻³.

questions.question: If the units of force and length are each doubled, the unit of energy becomes
questions.explanation: E = F × L, so the new unit = (2F)(2L) = 4 times the old unit. Note the subtlety: we're changing the SIZE of the unit, not of the quantity — so the numerical value of a given energy would fall to a quarter.

practiceSets.name: 🩺 NEET Drill — Motion in a Straight Line

questions.question: A car covers the first half of the distance at 30 km/h and the second half at 60 km/h. Its average speed is
questions.explanation: For equal DISTANCES, average speed = 2v₁v₂/(v₁+v₂) = 2(30)(60)/90 = 40 km/h. (For equal TIMES it would simply be the arithmetic mean, 45 km/h.)

questions.question: The area under a velocity–time graph gives
questions.explanation: Area under v–t = ∫v dt = displacement (signed). Area under a–t gives change in velocity, and the slope of v–t gives acceleration.

questions.question: The slope of a position–time graph gives
questions.explanation: dx/dt = velocity — the instantaneous slope. A curved x–t graph means changing velocity (non-zero acceleration).

questions.question: A body is thrown vertically upward with 20 m/s (g = 10 m/s²). Its time of flight is
questions.explanation: T = 2u/g = 2(20)/10 = 4 s. The time to reach the top is u/g = 2 s and the descent mirrors it exactly (for the same level).

questions.question: A car moving at 20 m/s stops in 5 s. Its retardation is
questions.explanation: a = (v − u)/t = (0 − 20)/5 = −4 m/s². The magnitude of the deceleration is 4 m/s² — the minus sign only indicates direction opposite to motion.

questions.question: A body falls freely from rest for 5 s (g = 10 m/s²). The distance fallen is
questions.explanation: s = ½gt² = ½(10)(25) = 125 m. Note that the distance grows as t², so each successive second covers more ground than the last.

questions.question: The velocity of a freely falling body after 3 s from rest (g = 10 m/s²) is
questions.explanation: v = gt = 10 × 3 = 30 m/s, directed downward. For free fall the initial speed is zero and gravity alone sets the acceleration.

questions.question: For a round trip that ends at the starting point, which quantity is ZERO?
questions.explanation: Displacement depends only on the endpoints, which coincide → zero. Distance is path length, which is never zero for a real trip — the classic distinction between the two.

questions.question: If a body moves with CONSTANT velocity, its acceleration is
questions.explanation: Constant velocity means no change in speed or direction, so a = 0. A body can have zero acceleration and still be moving — the commonest conceptual trap in this chapter.

questions.question: The distance travelled in the nth second is given by
questions.explanation: sₙ = u + ½a(2n − 1). It comes from subtracting s(n) − s(n−1) of the second equation of motion — and it's the standard tool for 'body covers 6 m in the 2nd second…' problems.

practiceSets.name: JEE Drill A — Kinematic equations & graphs

questions.question: x = 4t² − 2t (SI units). The velocity at t = 2 s is
questions.explanation: v = dx/dt = 8t − 2. At t = 2: v = 16 − 2 = 14 m/s. Differentiate first, then substitute — never substitute then differentiate.

questions.question: A car moving with speed v can be stopped in distance s. If its speed is doubled, the stopping distance becomes
questions.explanation: Using v² = u² − 2as with v = 0: s = u²/2a → s ∝ u². Doubling u makes s four times larger. This quadratic dependence is why speed limits matter so much more than people expect.

questions.question: A ball is dropped from a height and, at the same instant, another is thrown horizontally from the same height. They reach the ground
questions.explanation: Vertical motion is identical in both cases (initial vertical velocity zero, acceleration g); the horizontal throw doesn't affect the fall time. This is the independence of horizontal and vertical motion.

questions.question: A particle's position is x = t² (SI). Its average velocity between t = 0 and t = 2 s is
questions.explanation: Average velocity = Δx/Δt = (4 − 0)/2 = 2 m/s. (The instantaneous velocity at t = 2 s is 4 m/s — a common distractor.)

questions.question: A body covers 6 m in the 2nd second and 10 m in the 4th second. Its acceleration is
questions.explanation: sₙ = u + ½a(2n−1): u + 1.5a = 6 and u + 3.5a = 10 → 2a = 4 → a = 2 m/s² (and u = 3 m/s). Subtracting the two equations is the fastest route.

questions.question: A car decelerating uniformly at 2 m/s² from 10 m/s covers 21 m. Its final speed is
questions.explanation: v² = u² + 2as = 100 + 2(−2)(21) = 100 − 84 = 16 → v = 4 m/s. With deceleration the sign of a must be negative in the equation — the classic source of errors here.

questions.question: A body starts from rest with uniform acceleration. The ratio of the distance covered in the first 2 s to that covered in the next 2 s is
questions.explanation: s ∝ t² from rest: distances at t = 2 and t = 4 are in ratio 4:16, so the first interval is 4 and the second is 16 − 4 = 12 → 1:3. The odd-number ratio 1:3:5:7 is a famous Galileo result.

questions.question: Two trains 100 m and 150 m long move in OPPOSITE directions at 10 m/s and 15 m/s. The time they take to cross each other is
questions.explanation: Relative speed = 10 + 15 = 25 m/s, total distance to clear = 100 + 150 = 250 m → t = 250/25 = 10 s. For opposite directions you ADD the speeds; for the same direction you subtract.

practiceSets.name: JEE Drill B — Relative motion, graphs & free fall

questions.question: Two trains move in the SAME direction at 40 km/h and 30 km/h. The relative velocity of the faster with respect to the slower is
questions.explanation: Same direction → subtract: 40 − 30 = 10 km/h. Relative velocity is always v₁ − v₂ measured from the second body's frame.

questions.question: A ball is thrown vertically upward from the top of a tower with 10 m/s and reaches the ground in 5 s (g = 10 m/s²). The height of the tower is
questions.explanation: Take upward as positive: s = ut − ½gt² = 10(5) − ½(10)(25) = 50 − 125 = −75 m. The displacement is 75 m downward, so the tower is 75 m tall. Sign discipline solves these in one line.

questions.question: A body starting from rest with uniform acceleration covers distance s in time t. The distance covered in the NEXT t seconds is
questions.explanation: From rest, s ∝ t²: at time t the distance is s, at 2t it is 4s. So the second interval covers 4s − s = 3s. Same 1:3 logic as the earlier ratio question.

questions.question: A particle's velocity decreases uniformly from 20 m/s to zero in 10 s. The distance travelled is
questions.explanation: Distance = average velocity × time = ((20 + 0)/2)(10) = 100 m. Equivalently, it's the area of the v–t triangle — two ways of getting the same answer.

questions.question: For a body with v = 3t² (SI), the acceleration at t = 2 s is
questions.explanation: a = dv/dt = 6t = 12 m/s². Here acceleration itself grows with time — a reminder that dv/dt needn't be constant.

questions.question: A ball dropped from height h rebounds to h/4. Its speed just after the bounce, compared with just before, is
questions.explanation: v = √(2gh) so v ∝ √h: √(h/4)/√h = ½. The impact velocity halves — which is exactly why a bouncing ball's height falls off so fast.

questions.question: A stone is dropped from rest from a height. What is the ratio of the distances covered in the 1st, 2nd and 3rd seconds?
questions.explanation: sₙ = ½g(2n−1) ∝ (2n − 1) → 1:3:5. The sum of the first n odd numbers is n², which is exactly why total distance ∝ t².

questions.question: A particle has x = 3 + 6t + 4t² (SI). Its acceleration is
questions.explanation: v = 6 + 8t, a = 8 m/s² (constant). Comparing with x = x₀ + ut + ½at², the coefficient of t² is ½a = 4 → a = 8 — you can also read it straight off the equation.

practiceSets.name: 🩺 NEET Drill — Motion in a Plane

questions.question: For a projectile, the horizontal range is maximum when the angle of projection is
questions.explanation: R = u²sin2θ/g is maximised when sin2θ = 1, i.e. 2θ = 90° → θ = 45°. At 90° the range would be zero (straight up).

questions.question: A projectile is fired at 20 m/s at 30° to the horizontal (g = 10 m/s²). Its time of flight is
questions.explanation: T = 2u sinθ/g = 2(20)(0.5)/10 = 2 s. Only the vertical component u sinθ matters for the flight time.

questions.question: For the same projectile (u = 20 m/s, θ = 30°, g = 10), the maximum height is
questions.explanation: H = u²sin²θ/2g = (400)(0.25)/20 = 5 m. The vertical component is u sinθ = 10 m/s, and H = u_y²/2g = 100/20 = 5 m — a quick cross-check.

questions.question: The range of a projectile launched at 20 m/s at 30° (g = 10 m/s²) is closest to
questions.explanation: R = u²sin2θ/g = (400)(sin60°)/10 = 40 × 0.866 = 34.6 m (= 20√3 m). Note sin2θ = sin60°, not sin30° — the double-angle step is where marks are lost.

questions.question: At the highest point of a projectile's path, its velocity is
options: horizontal and equal to u cosθ
questions.explanation: The vertical component becomes zero at the top while the horizontal component u cosθ is unchanged throughout (no horizontal force). Only if θ = 90° would the velocity be zero at the top.

questions.question: A particle moves in a circle of radius 5 m with a constant speed of 10 m/s. Its centripetal acceleration is
questions.explanation: a_c = v²/r = 100/5 = 20 m/s², directed towards the centre. In uniform circular motion the speed is constant but the direction of velocity changes — hence the acceleration.

questions.question: In uniform circular motion, which of the following remains constant?
questions.explanation: Only the SPEED is constant; velocity, acceleration and momentum all keep changing direction. That's precisely why uniform circular motion is accelerated motion.

questions.question: A body completes one revolution in 2 s. Its angular velocity is
questions.explanation: ω = 2π/T = 2π/2 = π rad/s. Angular velocity depends on the period only — the radius doesn't enter.

questions.question: If a projectile is fired at 30° and another at 60° with the same speed, they have
questions.explanation: Complementary angles (θ and 90° − θ) give equal ranges because sin2θ = sin(180° − 2θ). Their heights and flight times, however, differ: the steeper one goes higher and stays longer.

questions.question: To cross a river in the SHORTEST TIME, a boat should head
questions.explanation: Shortest time means maximising the velocity component across the river — so point the boat straight across. The current then simply drifts you downstream (giving the shortest PATH only if you head upstream to compensate).

questions.question: A projectile has maximum height H and range R. If R = 4H, the angle of projection is
questions.explanation: R/H = (u²sin2θ/g)/(u²sin²θ/2g) = 4cosθ/sinθ → 4H·cotθ = R gives R/H = 4cotθ... using R = 4H → 4H = 4H·cotθ·... carefully: H = u²sin²θ/2g and R = u²sin2θ/g → R/H = 2sin2θ/sin²θ = 4cotθ. Setting R/H = 4 → cotθ = 1 → θ = 45°.

questions.question: A ball is thrown horizontally at 10 m/s from a height of 20 m (g = 10 m/s²). Its horizontal range is
questions.explanation: Fall time t = √(2h/g) = √4 = 2 s; range = u·t = 10 × 2 = 20 m. Horizontal launch means the vertical motion is pure free fall and the horizontal speed stays constant.

questions.question: For the same launch speed, the ratio of the maximum heights at 30° and 60° is
questions.explanation: H ∝ sin²θ, so H(30°)/H(60°) = (0.5)²/(0.866)² = 0.25/0.75 = 1:3. Steeper launch → much greater height.

questions.question: A projectile's speed at the highest point is n times the launch speed. Then cosθ equals
questions.explanation: At the top, v = u cosθ, so u cosθ = nu → cosθ = n. The horizontal component is what survives — a neat, memorisable relation.

questions.question: The change in velocity of a projectile between launch and landing (on the same level) is
questions.explanation: In magnitude: Δv = √((u cosθ − u cosθ)² + (−u sinθ − u sinθ)²) = 2u sinθ, directed downward. This equals g × time of flight — gravity alone changes the velocity. Direction: it's purely vertical since the horizontal component is unchanged.

questions.question: A projectile launched at 45° has a range of 100 m. Its maximum height is
questions.explanation: At 45°, R = 4H → H = R/4 = 25 m. Using the formula: H = u²/4g and R = u²/g, so R = 4H exactly.

questions.question: A stone whirled in a horizontal circle of radius 2 m at 4 m/s has angular speed
questions.explanation: ω = v/r = 4/2 = 2 rad/s. The linear speed is proportional to radius for the same ω — that's why points at the tip of a fan blade move faster than points near the hub.

questions.question: At the highest point of a projectile's trajectory, the angle between its velocity and acceleration is
questions.explanation: Velocity is horizontal and acceleration (g) is vertically downward → 90°. Throughout the flight, g is vertical while velocity turns from upward to downward.

practiceSets.name: JEE Drill B — Circular motion & relative velocity

questions.question: The maximum safe speed of a car on a banked frictionless road of radius r and banking angle θ is
questions.explanation: Balancing the vertical and centripetal directions: N cosθ = mg and N sinθ = mv²/r → v = √(rg tanθ). Banking lets the normal force supply the centripetal force that friction would otherwise provide.

questions.question: A river is 100 m wide. A boat that can move at 5 m/s in still water must cross in the shortest time with a 3 m/s current. The time is
questions.explanation: For shortest time, head straight across: t = width/boat speed = 100/5 = 20 s. The current only shifts the landing point downstream (by 3 × 20 = 60 m) — it doesn't affect the crossing time.

questions.question: Rain falls vertically at 4 m/s and a man walks at 3 m/s. The angle at which he should hold his umbrella from the vertical is
questions.explanation: tanθ = v_man/v_rain = 3/4 → θ ≈ 37°. The umbrella must point along the relative velocity of rain with respect to the man — a pure vector-subtraction problem.

questions.question: A particle in NON-uniform circular motion has
questions.explanation: Changing speed gives tangential acceleration (dv/dt), and moving in a circle always gives centripetal acceleration (v²/r). The net acceleration is their vector sum and no longer points at the centre.

questions.question: A stone in a vertical circle of radius 1 m needs a minimum speed at the TOP of
questions.explanation: At the top, gravity alone must supply the centripetal force: mg = mv²/r → v_min = √(gr) = √10 ≈ 3.16 m/s. The minimum speed at the BOTTOM is √(5gr) — don't swap the two.

questions.question: Angular velocity changes uniformly from 2 to 8 rad/s in 3 s. The angular acceleration is
questions.explanation: α = Δω/t = 6/3 = 2 rad/s². Angular kinematics mirrors linear kinematics: ω = ω₀ + αt, θ = ω₀t + ½αt².

questions.question: Two cars leave the same point with velocities 3 m/s east and 4 m/s north. After 5 s their separation is
questions.explanation: Relative velocity = √(3² + 4²) = 5 m/s (perpendicular components add in quadrature). Distance = 5 × 5 = 25 m.

questions.question: A cyclist going around a curve of radius 20 m at 10 m/s leans inward. His centripetal acceleration is
questions.explanation: a = v²/r = 100/20 = 5 m/s². The lean angle satisfies tanθ = v²/rg = 0.5 → θ = tan⁻¹(0.5) ≈ 27°. The lean is what allows friction to provide the centripetal force.

questions.question: Newton's first law of motion is also called the law of
questions.explanation: A body continues in its state of rest or uniform motion unless acted upon by a net external force — that IS the statement of inertia, which is why the third law is separately called the action–reaction law.

questions.question: A force of 10 N acts on a body of mass 2 kg. Its acceleration is
questions.explanation: a = F/m = 10/2 = 5 m/s². Newton's second law in its simplest form — watch that the force is the NET force, not one of several.

questions.question: Action and reaction forces
options: act on the same body and cancel out
act on different bodies and cancel out
act on different bodies and cannot cancel each other
questions.explanation: They're equal and opposite but act on DIFFERENT bodies, so they never cancel. If they acted on the same body, nothing could ever accelerate — a favourite conceptual trap.

questions.question: A force of 20 N acts for 0.5 s on a 2 kg body initially at rest. Its final velocity is
questions.explanation: Impulse = FΔt = 10 N·s = Δp = mv → v = 5 m/s. Alternatively a = 10 m/s² for 0.5 s gives v = 5 m/s — both routes are the same theorem.

questions.question: If the coefficient of friction is 0.5 and the normal reaction is 20 N, the friction force is
questions.explanation: f = μN = 0.5 × 20 = 10 N. Remember this is the LIMITING value — static friction equals the applied force until it hits this ceiling.

questions.question: The apparent weight of a person in a lift accelerating UPWARD with acceleration a is
questions.explanation: The floor must both support the weight and accelerate the person: N = m(g + a) > mg. In a lift accelerating downward it's m(g − a), and in free fall (a = g) it's zero — apparent weightlessness.

questions.question: Static friction is
options: self-adjusting and equal to the applied force up to a maximum
zero when the body is at rest
questions.explanation: Static friction varies from 0 up to μ_sN, exactly matching whatever force is applied. Only at impending motion does it reach its maximum — kinetic friction then takes over at a slightly lower constant value.

questions.question: The maximum speed of a car on a level circular road of radius r with coefficient of friction μ is
questions.explanation: Friction provides the centripetal force: μmg = mv²/r → v = √(μrg). On a level road, higher speed needs either a bigger radius or a larger μ (better tyres/dry road).

questions.question: A body of mass 5 kg has momentum 20 kg m/s. Its kinetic energy is
questions.explanation: K = p²/2m = 400/10 = 40 J. This p–K relation is the fastest route whenever momentum is given instead of velocity.

questions.question: Newton's third law follows directly from
questions.explanation: If forces always come in equal-opposite pairs acting on different bodies, the total momentum of an isolated system cannot change. That's the deep link between the third law and momentum conservation.

practiceSets.name: JEE Drill A — Pulleys, blocks & friction numericals

questions.question: Masses of 5 kg and 3 kg hang over a frictionless pulley. The acceleration of the system is (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂) = (2)(10)/(8) = 2.5 m/s², with the heavier mass moving down. The tension works out to 2m₁m₂g/(m₁+m₂) = 37.5 N — often the second part of the question.

questions.question: Blocks of 2 kg and 3 kg connected by a string are pulled on a frictionless surface by 10 N applied to the 2 kg block. The tension in the string is
questions.explanation: a = 10/5 = 2 m/s². The string must accelerate the 3 kg block, so T = 3 × 2 = 6 N. Take the body you DON'T have to worry about and apply F = ma.

questions.question: A 10 kg block slides down a frictionless incline of 30°. Its acceleration is (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: On a frictionless incline a = g sinθ = 10 × 0.5 = 5 m/s². The mass cancels — a lovely example of why the mass never appears in such answers.

questions.question: The angle of repose for a surface with μ = 1/√3 is
questions.explanation: tanθ = μ = 1/√3 → θ = 30°. The angle of repose is exactly the incline angle at which a block starts to slide on its own.

questions.question: A 2 kg block on a rough floor (μ = 0.2) is pushed with 10 N horizontally (g = 10 m/s²). Its acceleration is
questions.explanation: Friction = μmg = 0.2 × 20 = 4 N, so net force = 10 − 4 = 6 N → a = 3 m/s². Subtract friction BEFORE dividing by mass — the classic error is to divide first.

questions.question: An elevator of mass 1000 kg accelerates upward at 2 m/s² (g = 10 m/s²). The tension in the cable is
questions.explanation: T = m(g + a) = 1000(12) = 12,000 N. For downward acceleration it would be m(g − a) = 8000 N — the same formula with a sign change.

questions.question: A 5 kg block rests on a 10 kg block on a frictionless floor; μ between the blocks is 0.4. The maximum force (applied to the 10 kg block) so they move together is (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: The top block's motion comes only from friction: f_max = μmg = 0.4 × 50 = 20 N, so a_max = 20/5 = 4 m/s². Then F = (total mass) × a = 15 × 4 = 60 N. The limiting factor is always the block held by friction alone.

questions.question: A constant force gives a 4 kg body (initially at rest) a velocity of 15 m/s in 3 s. The force is
questions.explanation: a = 15/3 = 5 m/s², F = ma = 4 × 5 = 20 N. Or by impulse: Δp = 60 kg m/s over 3 s → 20 N. Total force needed = F_net.

practiceSets.name: JEE Drill B — Lifts, pseudo forces & circular motion

questions.question: A weighing machine in a lift reads a value m(g − a) when the lift
questions.explanation: The normal reaction (the reading) is N = m(g − a) for downward acceleration. At constant velocity or rest it reads mg — acceleration, not velocity, changes the reading.

questions.question: Three blocks of 1 kg, 2 kg and 3 kg are in contact on a frictionless surface. A force of 12 N pushes the 1 kg block. The contact force between the 2 kg and 3 kg blocks is
questions.explanation: a = 12/6 = 2 m/s². The 2–3 contact force only has to accelerate the 3 kg block: F = 3 × 2 = 6 N. Work backwards from the block on the far side.

questions.question: A body of mass m in a frame accelerating with 'a' experiences a pseudo force of
options: ma, opposite to the acceleration of the frame
ma, along the acceleration of the frame
questions.explanation: Pseudo forces aren't real forces — they appear only because the frame itself is accelerating. They always point opposite to the frame's acceleration, and they let you apply Newton's laws in non-inertial frames.

questions.question: A car of mass 500 kg takes a turn of radius 40 m on a level road with μ = 0.5 (g = 10 m/s²). The maximum safe speed is
questions.explanation: v = √(μrg) = √(0.5 × 40 × 10) = √200 ≈ 14.1 m/s ≈ 51 km/h. The mass cancels out of the calculation — a point NEET loves to test.

questions.question: A car crosses the top of a circular hill of radius R at the minimum possible speed. That speed is
questions.explanation: At the top, gravity supplies the centripetal force: mg = mv²/R → v = √(gR). Any faster and the car loses contact (leaves the road); any slower and it can't maintain the circular path.

questions.question: A 2 kg body at 3 m/s strikes and sticks to a stationary 1 kg body. Their common final speed is
questions.explanation: Momentum conservation: 2(3) = 3(v) → v = 2 m/s. In a perfectly inelastic collision momentum survives but kinetic energy does not: KE falls from 9 J to 6 J.

questions.question: A cricket ball of mass 0.2 kg moving at 20 m/s is brought to rest in 0.1 s. The average force is
questions.explanation: F = Δp/Δt = (0.2 × 20)/0.1 = 40 N. Note the direction: the force is opposite to the ball's motion — and this is exactly why catchers pull their hands back (longer Δt, smaller force).

questions.question: A block stays stationary on a rough incline. Then
options: friction equals mg sinθ only if θ = 45°
questions.explanation: The block is in equilibrium when mg sinθ ≤ μmg cosθ → tanθ ≤ μ. Beyond that angle (the angle of repose) it starts to slide — this inequality is the core of every 'will it slide?' question.

questions.question: The work done by a centripetal force in uniform circular motion is
questions.explanation: The force is always perpendicular to the displacement, so W = Fd cos90° = 0. That's exactly why the speed never changes even though the direction does — a beautifully consistent result.

questions.question: The work done by a force of 10 N in producing a displacement of 5 m at 60° to the force is
questions.explanation: W = Fd cosθ = 10 × 5 × 0.5 = 25 J. cos0° gives the maximum (50 J) and cos180° the most negative — the angle between force and displacement does all the work here.

questions.question: The kinetic energy of a 2 kg body moving at 10 m/s is
questions.explanation: K = ½mv² = ½(2)(100) = 100 J. Double the speed and the KE quadruples — the v² is where the quadratic cost of speed comes from.

questions.question: If the momentum of a body is doubled, its kinetic energy becomes
questions.explanation: K = p²/2m → K ∝ p². So doubling p quadruples K. This is why braking distance (which depends on energy) grows as the square of speed.

questions.question: The work–energy theorem states that the net work done on a body equals
questions.explanation: W_net = ΔK = ½mv² − ½mu². It's just Newton's second law integrated over displacement, and it's the go-to tool whenever speeds and distances (not times) are given.

questions.question: The potential energy stored in a spring of k = 200 N/m compressed by 0.1 m is
questions.explanation: U = ½kx² = ½(200)(0.01) = 1 J. The quadratic in x again: compressing twice as far stores four times the energy.

questions.question: If 100 J of work is done in 5 s, the average power is
questions.explanation: P = W/t = 20 W. Instantaneous power is P = F·v, which is why a car needs a bigger engine to hold high speed against drag.

questions.question: 1 kilowatt-hour equals
questions.explanation: 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. It's the commercial unit of energy — the one on your electricity bill.

questions.question: Which of the following is a NON-conservative force?
questions.explanation: Friction dissipates energy and its work depends on the path taken. Gravity, spring and electrostatic forces are conservative — work done around a closed loop is zero for them.

questions.question: A body is dropped from height h. Its speed just before hitting the ground is
questions.explanation: Energy conservation: mgh = ½mv² → v = √(2gh), independent of mass. That's why a coin and a cannonball hit the ground at the same speed (in vacuum).

practiceSets.name: JEE Drill A — Energy conservation & numericals

questions.question: A body slides down a smooth incline of height h. Its speed at the bottom is
questions.explanation: Energy conservation gives ½mv² = mgh for ANY frictionless path, so the angle, the length and the shape of the incline don't matter — only the vertical drop does. This is the most reused idea in the chapter.

questions.question: A 1 kg block moving at 4 m/s on a rough floor stops after 2 m. The work done by friction is
questions.explanation: By the work–energy theorem, W_friction = 0 − ½(1)(16) = −8 J. Friction removes 8 J of kinetic energy over those 2 m (so the average friction force is 4 N).

questions.question: A 0.1 kg bullet at 100 m/s embeds in a 0.9 kg block on a frictionless surface. The loss in kinetic energy is
questions.explanation: Momentum: 0.1(100) = 1.0(v) → v = 10 m/s. KE_i = 500 J, KE_f = ½(1)(100) = 50 J → loss = 450 J. Almost all the energy goes into heat and deformation — perfectly inelastic collisions are terribly wasteful.

questions.question: The power of a pump that raises 100 kg of water through 10 m in 20 s is (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: P = mgh/t = (100)(10)(10)/20 = 500 W. This is the OUTPUT power; a real pump would need more input power because of efficiency losses.

questions.question: The minimum speed at the bottom of a vertical circle of radius R for the body to complete the loop is
questions.explanation: At the top you need v_top = √(gR); conserving energy down to the bottom adds 4gR: v_bottom² = gR + 4gR = 5gR. The pair √(gR) at the top and √(5gR) at the bottom is a standard NEET ask.

questions.question: A force F = 3x N acts on a particle. The work done in moving it from x = 0 to x = 2 m is
questions.explanation: W = ∫F dx = ∫3x dx = 3x²/2 from 0 to 2 = 6 J. For variable forces, integrate (or find the area under the F–x graph) — you cannot use W = Fd directly.

questions.question: A ball dropped from 20 m loses 25% of its energy on bouncing. It rebounds to a height of
questions.explanation: Remaining energy = 75% of mgh → the new height is 0.75 × 20 = 15 m. Energy (not velocity) scales linearly with the retained fraction, since h ∝ energy.

questions.question: An engine moves a car at a constant 20 m/s against a resistive force of 500 N. The power delivered is
questions.explanation: At constant velocity the engine force must equal the resistance: P = Fv = 500 × 20 = 10,000 W = 10 kW. Note that zero net force does NOT mean zero power — a subtle and frequently examined point.

practiceSets.name: JEE Drill B — Collisions, springs & power

questions.question: A pendulum bob released from a horizontal position swings down. Its speed at the lowest point is
questions.explanation: The bob falls through a height L: mgh = ½mv² with h = L → v = √(2gL). For a release from angle θ it would be v = √(2gL(1 − cosθ)) — smoother and slower.

questions.question: Two bodies have the same kinetic energy but masses in the ratio 1 : 4. The ratio of their momenta is
questions.explanation: p = √(2mK), so p ∝ √m at equal K: √1 : √4 = 1 : 2. The heavier body carries more momentum for the same energy — which is why heavy vehicles are so destructive at low speeds.

questions.question: A moving body collides elastically head-on with an identical body at rest. After the collision
options: the first stops and the second remains at rest
questions.explanation: With equal masses one at rest: v₁' = 0 and v₂' = u₁. The moving body stops dead and the stationary one takes off with the same speed — the classic billiards result.

questions.question: A 2 kg block moving at 3 m/s hits a spring of k = 300 N/m on a frictionless surface. The maximum compression is
questions.explanation: ½mv² = ½kx² → ½(2)(9) = ½(300)x² → x² = 0.06 → x ≈ 0.245 m. At maximum compression the block is momentarily at rest, so ALL the KE has become spring PE.

questions.question: A constant 5 N force acts on a 2 kg body starting from rest for 4 s. The work done is
questions.explanation: a = 2.5 m/s², s = ½(2.5)(16) = 20 m, W = Fs = 100 J. Cross-check with the work–energy theorem: v = 10 m/s → K = ½(2)(100) = 100 J ✓

questions.question: The work done by gravity on a body that moves once around a closed loop is
questions.explanation: Gravity is conservative: the net work over a closed path is zero because the vertical displacement is zero. That's the defining property of any conservative force.

questions.question: A lift of mass 500 kg rises 20 m in 10 s at constant speed (g = 10 m/s²). The power of the motor is
questions.explanation: P = mgh/t = (500)(10)(20)/10 = 10,000 W = 10 kW. At constant speed the motor only needs to balance gravity — no extra power for acceleration.

questions.question: In a perfectly inelastic collision between equal masses (one at rest), the fraction of kinetic energy lost is
questions.explanation: Momentum gives v = u/2, so KE_f = ½(2m)(u/2)² = ¼mu² versus KE_i = ½mu² → exactly half is lost. Perfectly inelastic collisions waste the most energy while conserving momentum.

questions.question: The moment of inertia of a solid sphere about a diameter is
questions.explanation: Solid sphere about a diameter: (2/5)MR². The hollow sphere is (2/3)MR² — the pair that NEET loves to swap.

questions.question: The moment of inertia of a disc about an axis through its centre perpendicular to its plane is
questions.explanation: Disc: ½MR²; ring of the same mass and radius: MR². Mass distributed further out means a larger MI.

questions.question: A dancer folds her arms while spinning. Her angular velocity
options: increases because I decreases (L is conserved)
questions.explanation: With no external torque, L = Iω is constant, so reducing I increases ω. This is also why a raw egg spins slower than a boiled one.

questions.question: The torque acting on a body is
questions.explanation: τ = rF sinθ, maximum when the force is perpendicular to the radius. Note that only the perpendicular component of F produces torque.

questions.question: The centre of mass of a uniform rod lies
questions.explanation: Symmetry puts the COM of a uniform rod at its geometric centre. The MI about the end is (1/3)ML² while about the centre it's (1/12)ML².

questions.question: For a body rolling without slipping on a surface
questions.explanation: Rolling without slipping means the contact point is instantaneously at rest, so the centre moves at v = ωR. If slipping occurred, this relation would break.

questions.question: The total kinetic energy of a rolling body is
questions.explanation: Rolling is translation plus rotation simultaneously, so both terms count. For a disc, the rotational share is exactly one-third of the total.

questions.question: Which quantity is conserved when the net external torque is zero?
questions.explanation: τ_net = dL/dt, so zero torque means constant L. If no external force acts, linear momentum is also conserved — but KE need not be (a skater's muscles do work).

practiceSets.name: JEE Drill — MI, rolling & axis theorems

questions.question: The moment of inertia of a uniform rod of mass M and length L about an axis through one end perpendicular to it is
questions.explanation: About the end: ML²/3; about the centre: ML²/12. Parallel axis theorem gives ML²/12 + M(L/2)² = ML²/3 ✓

questions.question: Two masses of 2 kg and 3 kg are placed at x = 0 and x = 5 m. Their centre of mass is at
questions.explanation: X_CM = (2×0 + 3×5)/5 = 15/5 = 3 m. The heavier mass pulls the COM towards itself — always check the answer sits between the particles.

questions.question: The moment of inertia of a hollow sphere about a diameter is
questions.explanation: Hollow sphere: (2/3)MR² > solid sphere's (2/5)MR². This is why a hollow sphere rolls down an incline slower than a solid one of the same size.

questions.question: A solid sphere rolls down an incline of angle θ without slipping. Its acceleration is
questions.explanation: a = g sinθ/(1 + I/MR²) = g sinθ/(1 + 2/5) = (5/7)g sinθ. For a disc it would be (2/3)g sinθ, and for a ring g sinθ/2 — the smaller the I/MR², the faster it rolls.

questions.question: The moment of inertia of a disc of mass M and radius R about a diameter is
questions.explanation: By the perpendicular axis theorem, I_z = I_x + I_y = MR²/2, and symmetry gives I_x = I_y = MR²/4. The perpendicular axis theorem only applies to planar (lamina-type) bodies.

questions.question: For a rolling disc, the fraction of total kinetic energy that is rotational is
questions.explanation: KE_rot/KE_total = (I/MR²)/(1 + I/MR²) = (1/2)/(3/2) = 1/3 for a disc; it's 2/7 for a solid sphere and 1/2 for a ring.

questions.question: Angular momentum of a particle of mass m moving with velocity v at perpendicular distance r from a point is
questions.explanation: L = r × p = mvr sinθ. For circular motion this becomes L = mvr = mr²ω = Iω — the bridge between the particle and rigid-body pictures.

questions.question: A solid sphere and a hollow sphere of the same mass and radius roll down the same incline from rest. Which reaches the bottom first?
questions.explanation: Smaller I/MR² → larger acceleration: solid (2/5) beats hollow (2/3). Order for all bodies: solid sphere > disc > hollow sphere > ring, regardless of mass and radius.

questions.question: The universal gravitational constant G has the value
questions.explanation: G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² and it's a UNIVERSAL constant — its value doesn't change with place, medium or time. That's what makes it different from g.

questions.question: The value of g at the centre of the Earth is
questions.explanation: g = GM(r)/r² inside a uniform sphere gives g ∝ r, so g = 0 at the centre and maximum at the surface. That's why a body weighs the least at the Earth's centre.

questions.question: Escape velocity from the Earth's surface is approximately
questions.explanation: ve = √(2gR) = √(2 × 9.8 × 6.4×10⁶) ≈ 11.2 km/s, independent of the body's mass and direction of projection. The moon's is only about 2.4 km/s — which is why the moon can't hold an atmosphere.

questions.question: Kepler's third law states that
questions.explanation: The square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis. Its constants differ from planet to planet only through the mass of the central body.

questions.question: The orbital velocity of a satellite close to the Earth's surface is about
questions.explanation: vo = √(gR) ≈ 7.9 km/s and v_escape = √2 × vo ≈ 11.2 km/s. The factor √2 is the whole difference — and that's why escape needs only 41% more speed.

questions.question: An astronaut inside an orbiting satellite feels weightless because
options: the astronaut and satellite are both in free fall with the same acceleration
questions.explanation: Gravity is still substantial at satellite altitudes; it simply provides the centripetal force for BOTH. Since they fall together, the normal reaction is zero — apparent weightlessness, not zero gravity.

questions.question: If the mass of the Earth were doubled (same radius), g would
questions.explanation: g = GM/R², so g ∝ M for fixed R. Doubling the mass doubles g — and it would also raise the escape velocity by √2.

questions.question: The gravitational potential energy of two masses separated by distance r is
questions.explanation: The negative sign is crucial — it means the masses are bound, and energy must be SUPPLIED to separate them to infinity. The potential is taken as zero at infinite separation.

practiceSets.name: JEE Drill — g variation, satellites & energy

questions.question: At a height equal to the Earth's radius R, the value of g becomes
questions.explanation: g' = gR²/(R + h)² with h = R gives g' = g/4. Note that at depth R (the centre) g = 0 — height and depth scale very differently.

questions.question: The escape velocity from a planet with twice the Earth's mass and half the Earth's radius is
questions.explanation: ve = √(2GM/R) ∝ √(M/R) → √(2/0.5) = √4 = 2. So ve doubles to 22.4 km/s. The escape velocity scales as √(M/R), not linearly.

questions.question: The time period of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius r around a planet of mass M is
questions.explanation: Equating GMm/r² to mω²r and using ω = 2π/T gives T = 2π√(r³/GM). This is Kepler's third law in its general form — T² ∝ r³.

questions.question: The total energy of a satellite of mass m in an orbit of radius r is
questions.explanation: TE = KE + PE = GMm/2r − GMm/r = −GMm/2r. Its magnitude equals both the KE and half the PE — a trio worth memorising exactly.

questions.question: A geostationary satellite must orbit
options: in the equatorial plane from west to east with T = 24 h
in any plane with T = 24 h
in a polar plane with T = 12 h
questions.explanation: It must match the Earth's rotation both in period (24 h) and direction, and be above the equator so it can stay fixed over one point — hence its ~36,000 km altitude.

questions.question: The gravitational field inside a uniform solid sphere at a distance r from the centre is
questions.explanation: Only the mass enclosed within radius r contributes: g = GMr/R³ ∝ r. Outside the sphere it falls as 1/r² — the two regimes are the basis of the standard g-vs-r graph.

questions.question: The weight of a body at a depth d below the Earth's surface (d << R) is reduced by the fraction
questions.explanation: g' = g(1 − d/R), so the fractional decrease is d/R. Careful: at a HEIGHT h = d the decrease is 2d/R (twice as much) — the classic height-vs-depth trap.

questions.question: A satellite's kinetic energy is increased while it stays in orbit. Then its orbital radius
questions.explanation: Higher orbits have lower speed (v ∝ 1/√r) but higher total energy. This counterintuitive result — adding energy slows the satellite — appears constantly in JEE.

practiceSets.name: 🩺 NEET Drill — Mechanical Properties of Solids

questions.question: The SI unit of stress is
questions.explanation: Stress = force/area → N/m² = pascal. Strain is a pure ratio, so it has NO units — stress has the same units as pressure.

questions.question: Hooke's law is valid
questions.explanation: Stress ∝ strain holds only up to the proportional/elastic limit. Beyond the yield point the material deforms plastically and Hooke's law fails.

questions.question: Steel is more elastic than rubber because
options: steel has a much larger Young's modulus
questions.explanation: More elastic = larger Y = more stress needed for the same strain. Steel's Y ≈ 2 × 10¹¹ Pa versus rubber's ≈ 10⁶ Pa — so steel resists deformation far more.

questions.question: Young's modulus is defined as
questions.explanation: Y = (F/A)/(ΔL/L) = FL/AΔL. A higher Y means a stiffer material — diamond and steel sit at the top of the table.

questions.question: The bulk modulus of a perfectly rigid body is
questions.explanation: A rigid body shows zero volume strain no matter how much pressure is applied, and K = −P/(ΔV/V) → ∞. Compressibility = 1/K is then zero.

questions.question: The elastic potential energy per unit volume of a stretched wire is
questions.explanation: u = ½ × stress × strain = ½Y(strain)² = stress²/2Y. It's the area under the stress–strain line — exactly like ½kx² for a spring.

questions.question: Poisson's ratio for most materials lies between
questions.explanation: σ = lateral strain/longitudinal strain, typically 0.2–0.4 and theoretically never above 0.5 (that would mean the volume increases on stretching).

questions.question: The stretching of a wire beyond the elastic limit causes
options: the wire to return to its original length
questions.explanation: Past the yield point, plastic deformation sets in and the wire does not fully recover. That's the elastic-to-plastic transition visible on the stress–strain curve.

practiceSets.name: JEE Drill — Elongation, energy & thermal stress

questions.question: A wire of length L, area A and Young's modulus Y hangs from a support with a mass M attached. Its extension is
questions.explanation: ΔL = FL/AY = MgL/AY. Check dimensions and the trend: a longer, thinner wire stretches more, while a stiffer material stretches less.

questions.question: A wire of uniform cross-section hangs under its own weight. The extension due to its own weight is
questions.explanation: The tension varies linearly from Mg at the top to 0 at the bottom, so the average tension Mg/2 acts on the whole length — giving half the elongation of a rod with the same mass hung from its end.

questions.question: Two wires of the same material have lengths in the ratio 1:2 and areas in the ratio 1:2 under the same load. The ratio of their extensions is
questions.explanation: ΔL ∝ L/A, so the ratio is (1/1)/(2/2) = 1:1. Both length and area double, and their effects cancel exactly.

questions.question: The elastic potential energy stored in a wire of volume V, stress σ and Young's modulus Y is
questions.explanation: u = σ²/2Y per unit volume, so U = σ²V/2Y. Stretching a wire with a high Y then stores less energy for the same stress — which is why springs use low-Y, ductile materials.

questions.question: A wire is stretched by 1 mm under a load. If the same wire is halved in length and stretched by the same load, the extension becomes
questions.explanation: ΔL ∝ L, so halving the length halves the extension (assuming the same cross-sectional area). Length and extension are directly proportional under a fixed load.

questions.question: A steel rod is clamped between two rigid walls and heated. The thermal stress developed is
questions.explanation: Thermal stress = YαΔT. If the rod were free, it would expand by αΔT·L; the walls prevent that, effectively applying a compressive strain αΔT, which Hooke's law turns into a stress.

questions.question: A wire of length 2 m and area 10⁻⁶ m² stretches by 2 mm under a load of 100 N. Young's modulus is
questions.explanation: Y = FL/AΔL = (100 × 2)/(10⁻⁶ × 2×10⁻³) = 200/2×10⁻⁹ = 10¹¹ Pa — exactly the typical value for steel, a good sanity check.

questions.question: If a wire is stretched to double its original length within the elastic limit, the elastic energy stored becomes
questions.explanation: Energy density ∝ strain², so doubling the strain quadruples the energy per unit volume; the volume is unchanged, so the total stored energy roughly quadruples (more than double). This is why rubber bands snap dangerously when over-stretched.

practiceSets.name: 🩺 NEET Drill — Mechanical Properties of Fluids

questions.question: The pressure at a depth h in a liquid of density ρ is
questions.explanation: Total pressure = atmospheric + gauge pressure. Pressure at a point in a fluid is the same in all directions (isotropic) — that's why a diver feels pressure from every side.

questions.question: A body floats in a liquid when
options: its weight is less than the buoyant force
its weight equals the buoyant force
questions.explanation: For a floating body, upthrust = weight. Since upthrust = V_submerged ρ_liquid g, the fraction submerged equals the ratio of the body's density to the liquid's.

questions.question: The equation of continuity for an incompressible fluid states
questions.explanation: Mass conservation means the volume flow rate is constant, so where the pipe narrows the fluid speeds up. That's the same principle that makes a river run faster in its shallows.

questions.question: Bernoulli's theorem is a statement of
options: Newton's second law for fluids only
conservation of energy for a flowing fluid
questions.explanation: P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant along a streamline — it's the work–energy theorem applied to a fluid element. It assumes ideal (non-viscous, incompressible, steady) flow.

questions.question: An aeroplane lifts because air flows faster over the upper surface, which
questions.explanation: Faster flow → lower pressure, so the higher pressure below the wing provides net upward lift. Atomiser sprayers and the Venturi meter use the same principle.

questions.question: The terminal velocity of a sphere falling in a viscous fluid is proportional to
options: the square of the sphere's radius
questions.explanation: v_t = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/9η ∝ r². That's why fine dust settles so slowly while a stone drops straight through water.

questions.question: Surface tension has the dimensions of
questions.explanation: T = F/L, units N/m, equivalent to energy per unit area (J/m²). It arises because surface molecules have fewer neighbours and hence higher energy.

questions.question: Capillary rise of a liquid in a tube of radius r is given by
questions.explanation: h = 2Tcosθ/ρgr, so h ∝ 1/r — narrower tubes raise the liquid higher. For mercury (θ > 90°) the same formula gives a negative h, which is the capillary depression.

practiceSets.name: JEE Drill — Bernoulli, viscosity & capillarity problems

questions.question: Water flows through a pipe of radius 2 cm at 1 m/s. Where the radius narrows to 1 cm, the velocity is
questions.explanation: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ with A ∝ r²: v₂ = v₁(r₁/r₂)² = 1 × 4 = 4 m/s. Halving the radius quadruples the speed — the area ratio is squared.

questions.question: Water flows from a tank through a hole at depth 5 m below the surface (g = 10 m/s²). The efflux speed is
questions.explanation: Torricelli's law: v = √(2gh) = √100 = 10 m/s — the same as the free-fall speed from that height. Note the answer doesn't depend on the hole's size or the liquid's density.

questions.question: A soap bubble of radius R has an excess pressure of
questions.explanation: A soap bubble has two surfaces, so ΔP = 4T/R; a liquid drop has only one, giving 2T/R. This factor of 2 is one of the most-tested details in the chapter.

questions.question: Two capillary tubes of radii r and 2r are dipped in the same liquid. The ratio of the liquid rises is
questions.explanation: h ∝ 1/r, so the thinner tube (r) shows twice the rise of the wider one (2r). This is the basis of the capillary-rise method for measuring surface tension.

questions.question: A drop of radius R breaks into 1000 droplets of equal size. The surface energy
questions.explanation: Volume conservation gives each small drop radius r = R/10, and total area goes up by a factor of 10. Since energy ∝ area, the surface energy increases tenfold — that's why liquids tend to form a single drop.

questions.question: The Reynolds number determines whether flow is
questions.explanation: Re = ρvD/η. Below about 2000 the flow is laminar; above 3000 it's turbulent. It compares inertial to viscous forces — a pure number, so it's dimensionless.

questions.question: An object of density 800 kg/m³ floats in water (1000 kg/m³). The fraction of its volume submerged is
questions.explanation: Fraction submerged = ρ_body/ρ_liquid = 800/1000 = 0.8. It's the same idea as the iceberg — 90% of an iceberg's volume sits below the waterline because ice is about 90% as dense as water.

questions.question: The terminal velocity of a small sphere in a liquid becomes constant because
options: the viscous drag plus buoyancy balances the weight
questions.explanation: At terminal velocity the net force is zero: mg = upthrust + 6πηrv_t. Before that, the sphere accelerates and the drag grows until balance is reached.

practiceSets.name: 🩺 NEET Drill — Thermal Properties of Matter

questions.question: The temperature −40 °C corresponds to
questions.explanation: C/5 = (F − 32)/9 with C = −40 gives F = −40 — the unique point where the two scales agree. Worth memorising as a quick sanity check.

questions.question: For a solid, the coefficient of volume expansion γ is related to the linear coefficient α by
questions.explanation: γ = 3α and β (areal) = 2α, because length, area and volume involve 1, 2 and 3 powers of the linear dimension. Watch out for questions that give β and ask for γ (γ = 3β/2).

questions.question: Water has its maximum density at
questions.explanation: Water anomalously contracts from 0 °C to 4 °C and expands above it. This is why lakes freeze from the top and fish survive underneath — a frequently asked 'anomalous expansion' question.

questions.question: The quantity of heat required to change 1 kg of ice at 0 °C into water at 0 °C is called
questions.explanation: Latent heat of fusion of ice = 80 cal/g = 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg. During melting the temperature stays at 0 °C — all the heat goes into breaking the lattice, not raising temperature.

questions.question: The SI unit of thermal conductivity is
questions.explanation: Q/t = kAΔT/L gives k = W m⁻¹ K⁻¹. Metals have high k (copper ~400) and gases/insulators low values — which is why air is a great insulator when trapped.

questions.question: Wien's displacement law states that
questions.explanation: λ_mT = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m·K. Hotter bodies radiate at shorter wavelengths — the reason a heated iron bar glows red, then yellow, then white as it gets hotter.

questions.question: According to Stefan's law, the energy radiated per unit area per unit time by a black body is proportional to
questions.explanation: E = σT⁴ with σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴. The fourth power makes this brutal: doubling the absolute temperature gives 16 times the radiated power.

questions.question: Newton's law of cooling states that the rate of loss of heat is proportional to
options: the absolute temperature of the body
the temperature difference between the body and surroundings
questions.explanation: dQ/dt ∝ (T − T₀), valid for small temperature differences. It's a linear approximation of Stefan's law and gives the exponential cooling curve.

practiceSets.name: JEE Drill — Calorimetry, conduction & radiation problems

questions.question: How much heat is needed to convert 100 g of ice at 0 °C to water at 0 °C? (L = 80 cal/g)
questions.explanation: Q = mL = 100 × 80 = 8000 cal. Note this raises the temperature by nothing at all — it's all latent heat. To then warm it to 20 °C you'd add 100 × 1 × 20 = 2000 cal more.

questions.question: Two rods of the same dimensions have thermal conductivities k and 2k and are joined in series. The effective conductivity is
questions.explanation: For series, 1/k_eff = (1/2)(1/k + 1/2k) → k_eff = 4k/3. Materials in series add thermal RESISTANCES, exactly like electrical resistors in series.

questions.question: A body cools from 60 °C to 50 °C in 10 min. The room temperature is 25 °C. The time to cool from 50 °C to 40 °C is
questions.explanation: The average excess temperature is lower in the second interval (45 − 25 = 20 vs 55 − 25 = 30), so cooling slows: it takes MORE than 10 min. This is the essence of Newton's law of cooling and a standard NEET reasoning question.

questions.question: A black body at 300 K radiates energy E. If its temperature rises to 600 K, the radiated energy becomes
questions.explanation: E ∝ T⁴ → (600/300)⁴ = 16. The fourth-power law is what makes stars vastly brighter than planets despite modest temperature differences.

questions.question: Two spheres of radii 1 cm and 2 cm are at the same temperature. The ratio of the energy radiated per second is
questions.explanation: Power ∝ surface area ∝ r² → 1:4. Temperature equality means the energy per unit AREA is the same, so only the areas matter.

questions.question: A metal rod 1 m long with cross-section 10⁻⁴ m² and k = 400 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ has ends at 100 °C and 0 °C. The heat current is
questions.explanation: Q/t = kAΔT/L = 400 × 10⁻⁴ × 100/1 = 4 W. This is Fourier's law of conduction — the steady-state heat current is analogous to current in Ohm's law.

questions.question: A body cools in a surrounding of 30 °C. Its temperature–time graph will be
questions.explanation: Newton's law gives dT/dt ∝ −(T − T₀), whose solution is T = T₀ + (T_i − T₀)e^(−kt) — an exponential approach that never quite reaches the ambient temperature.

questions.question: The temperature of the Sun's surface is about 5800 K. The wavelength of maximum emission is about
questions.explanation: λ_m = b/T = 2.9×10⁻³/5800 ≈ 5 × 10⁻⁷ m = 500 nm — right in the middle of the visible spectrum (green-blue). Human vision evolved to peak exactly where the Sun radiates most.

questions.question: The first law of thermodynamics is a statement of
questions.explanation: ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW. Heat supplied part goes into raising internal energy and part into doing work — nothing is lost, only redistributed.

questions.question: For an isothermal process,
questions.explanation: Constant temperature means the internal energy of an ideal gas doesn't change, so all the heat absorbed appears as work done. Isothermal requires the process to be very slow and the container conducting.

questions.question: For an adiabatic process,
questions.explanation: No heat is exchanged, so any work done by the gas comes out of its internal energy — which is why a gas expanding adiabatically cools. Adiabatic processes must be fast or well insulated.

questions.question: For an isochoric (constant volume) process,
questions.explanation: With no volume change, the gas does no work, so all the heat supplied raises the temperature: Q = nCvΔT. That's why heating in a closed rigid container raises pressure so effectively.

questions.question: The efficiency of a Carnot engine working between T₁ (source) and T₂ (sink) is
questions.explanation: η = 1 − T₂/T₁ with temperatures in KELVIN. The efficiency is 100% only if T₂ = 0 K, which is unattainable — the practical statement of the second law.

questions.question: For a cyclic process,
questions.explanation: Internal energy is a state function, so returning to the same state means ΔU = 0, and hence Q = W. On a P-V diagram, the net work is the area enclosed by the cycle.

questions.question: Cp − Cv for an ideal gas equals
questions.explanation: Mayer's relation: Cp − Cv = R (per mole). The extra heat capacity at constant pressure pays for the work of expansion against the atmosphere.

questions.question: A refrigerator's coefficient of performance is
questions.explanation: COP = heat extracted from the cold reservoir / work input = Q₂/W. For an ideal (Carnot) refrigerator, COP = T₂/(T₁ − T₂), which can be much greater than 1.

practiceSets.name: JEE Drill — Work, P-V graphs & engine problems

questions.question: Work done by a gas in an isobaric expansion from V₁ to V₂ at pressure P is
questions.explanation: At constant pressure, W = PΔV = nRΔT. On a P-V diagram this is simply the area of the rectangle under the process line — geometry replaces algebra in graph questions.

questions.question: Work done in an isothermal expansion of n moles at T from V to 2V is
questions.explanation: W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁) = nRT ln2 ≈ 0.693nRT. Isothermal work is the area under a hyperbolic curve — and it's always larger than the corresponding adiabatic work.

questions.question: For a monoatomic ideal gas, the value of γ = Cp/Cv is
questions.explanation: Monoatomic: Cv = 3R/2, Cp = 5R/2 → γ = 5/3. Diatomic: γ = 7/5; polyatomic: γ ≈ 4/3. The value of γ identifies the gas in 'unknown gas' questions.

questions.question: An engine absorbs 600 J from the source and rejects 400 J to the sink per cycle. Its efficiency is
questions.explanation: W = 600 − 400 = 200 J, so η = W/Q₁ = 200/600 = 33.3%. Always divide the net work by the heat ABSORBED from the source, never by the heat rejected.

questions.question: In an adiabatic expansion of an ideal gas, the temperature
questions.explanation: The gas uses its own internal energy to do work, so ΔU < 0 and T falls. This is why a CO₂ fire extinguisher's nozzle frosts over and why compressed air cools on release.

questions.question: The work done by a gas in a cyclic process equals
options: the area enclosed by the cycle on the P-V diagram
the area under the highest curve
questions.explanation: The net work is the enclosed area — positive for a clockwise cycle, negative for anticlockwise. Note that for a cycle W ≠ 0 even though ΔU = 0.

questions.question: A Carnot engine operates between 500 K and 300 K. Its efficiency is
questions.explanation: η = 1 − 300/500 = 0.4 = 40%. Note the answer depends only on the two temperatures (in K) — no property of the working substance enters.

questions.question: The second law of thermodynamics implies that
options: heat cannot flow from cold to hot under any circumstances
no engine can convert all absorbed heat into work
questions.explanation: Kelvin–Planck statement: a 100% efficient heat engine is impossible. Heat CAN flow from cold to hot when work is supplied — that's exactly what a refrigerator does.

practiceSets.name: 🩺 NEET Drill — Kinetic Theory of Gases

questions.question: The average kinetic energy of a molecule of an ideal gas is
questions.explanation: KE = (3/2)kT per molecule for a monoatomic gas (k = Boltzmann constant). With R and a mole it becomes (3/2)RT — the distinction between per-molecule and per-mole is a classic trap.

questions.question: The rms speed of gas molecules is given by
questions.explanation: v_rms = √(3RT/M) where M is the MOLAR MASS in kg/mol. The other two formulas give the average and most probable speeds — all three differ only in the constant under the root.

questions.question: The ratio v_rms : v_avg : v_mp for gas molecules is
questions.explanation: Numerically ≈ 1.73 : 1.60 : 1.41, so v_rms > v_avg > v_mp always. Remember the order — it's a standard one-mark question.

questions.question: The degrees of freedom of a diatomic gas at room temperature is
questions.explanation: 3 translational + 2 rotational = 5 (vibration is frozen out at room temperature). This gives Cv = 5R/2 and γ = 7/5 = 1.4 — the value for air.

questions.question: The pressure of an ideal gas is given by
questions.explanation: P = ⅓(mN/V)v²rms = ⅓ρv²rms. Pressure arises purely from molecular collisions with the walls — no molecules, no pressure.

questions.question: At absolute zero temperature, the kinetic energy of gas molecules is
questions.explanation: KE ∝ T, so classically it reaches zero at 0 K. Quantum mechanics adds a small zero-point energy, but the classical answer expected in exams is zero — and this is why 0 K is the 'motion stops' limit.

questions.question: The mean free path of gas molecules
questions.explanation: λ = kT/(√2 πd²P), so λ ∝ 1/P. Lower pressure means fewer molecules per unit volume and hence longer runs between collisions — the principle behind vacuum physics.

questions.question: Two gases at the same temperature have the same
questions.explanation: KE = (3/2)kT depends only on temperature, so it's equal for all gases at that temperature. But lighter molecules move faster — the same energy with less mass means more speed.

practiceSets.name: JEE Drill — Speeds, DOF & gas problems

questions.question: The rms speed of oxygen molecules at 300 K (M = 32 g/mol, R = 8.314) is about
questions.explanation: v_rms = √(3 × 8.314 × 300/0.032) = √(233,800) ≈ 484 m/s. Use M in kg/mol — leaving it in g/mol is the commonest error in these numericals.

questions.question: If the temperature of a gas is raised from 27 °C to 327 °C, the rms speed becomes
questions.explanation: Convert first: 300 K → 600 K. Since v ∝ √T, the speed rises by √2 ≈ 1.41. Note the temperature must ALWAYS be doubled in kelvin, not celsius.

questions.question: A mixture of 1 mole of He and 1 mole of H₂ is at temperature T. The ratio of their rms speeds is
questions.explanation: v ∝ 1/√M, so v_He/v_H₂ = √(2/4) = 1/√2 → the ratio is 1:√2... careful: H₂ is lighter so it's faster, giving v_He : v_H2 = √2 : 2 = 1 : √2. The lighter gas always wins.

questions.question: The specific heat at constant volume for a monoatomic gas is
questions.explanation: Cv = (f/2)R with f = 3 → 3R/2, and γ = 5/3 ≈ 1.67. For diatomic (f = 5): Cv = 5R/2, γ = 1.4 — the two values you'll use most in exams.

questions.question: If the pressure of a fixed amount of gas is doubled at constant temperature, the mean free path becomes
questions.explanation: λ ∝ T/P, so doubling P halves λ — molecules are packed twice as densely, so they collide twice as often. (Note the rms SPEED is unchanged, since T is constant.)

questions.question: The energy of a gas at temperature T with f degrees of freedom per molecule is
questions.explanation: Law of equipartition: each degree of freedom carries ½kT. So a diatomic gas (f = 5) has 5/2 kT per molecule — which explains why its Cv is larger.

questions.question: Equal masses of H₂ and O₂ are mixed at the same temperature. The ratio of their average kinetic energies is
questions.explanation: Average KE per molecule depends only on T, so it's identical: 1:1. Their speeds differ by a factor of 4 (v ∝ 1/√M with M in ratio 1:16) — that's the part of the question where molecules differ.

questions.question: A vessel contains gas at 1 atm. If the volume is halved at constant temperature, the number of collisions per unit area per second
questions.explanation: Halving the volume doubles the number density n. Pressure P = ⅓nmv²rms — with v_rms fixed (same T), P doubles because n doubled. Collision rate with the walls therefore doubles too.

quests.title: D+1 · Lock-in
quests.description: Redo 5 cold mistakes + state the SHM card aloud. 15 min.

questions.question: The time period of a simple pendulum depends on
options: its length and the value of g only
questions.explanation: T = 2π√(l/g) — mass and (for small swings) amplitude do not appear at all. That is why a pendulum clock keeps time as its bob wears out.

questions.question: A particle executing SHM with amplitude A has its maximum speed
questions.explanation: v = ω√(A² − x²) is largest at x = 0 (the mean position) where a = 0. At the extremes v = 0 while a is maximum.

questions.question: A body in SHM has amplitude 5 cm and time period 2 s. Its maximum acceleration is about
questions.explanation: ω = 2π/T = π rad/s, so a_max = ω²A = π² × 0.05 ≈ 0.49 m/s². Keep amplitude in metres.

questions.question: In SHM, the kinetic energy equals the potential energy at displacement x equal to
questions.explanation: KE = PE means PE = E/2, so ½kx² = ½ × ½kA² → x = A/√2. At x = A/2 the ratio KE : PE is 3 : 1 instead.

questions.question: If the mass attached to a spring is made four times, the time period becomes
questions.explanation: T = 2π√(m/k) → T ∝ √m. Quadrupling m multiplies T by √4 = 2.

questions.question: A pendulum keeps correct time on Earth. On the Moon, where g is 1/6 as large, its period becomes
questions.explanation: T ∝ 1/√g, so reducing g to g/6 multiplies the period by √6 ≈ 2.45 — the clock runs slow.

questions.question: In SHM the displacement and the acceleration at any instant are
questions.explanation: a = −ω²x — the minus sign means a always points towards the mean position, i.e. exactly opposite to the displacement.

questions.question: The total energy of a particle in SHM is proportional to
options: the square root of the amplitude
questions.explanation: E = ½mω²A², so E ∝ A² (and ∝ ω²). Doubling the amplitude quadruples the energy.

questions.question: A spring of force constant k is cut into two equal halves and a mass m is hung from one half. The time period is
questions.explanation: Half the length means twice the stiffness: k' = 2k. Then T' = 2π√(m/2k) = T/√2 ≈ 0.71T.

questions.question: Two springs, each of force constant k, are joined in series and a mass m is attached. The time period of oscillation is
questions.explanation: In series 1/k_eff = 1/k + 1/k → k_eff = k/2, so T = 2π√(m/(k/2)) = 2π√(2m/k), which is √2 times larger than a single spring.

questions.question: A particle in SHM of amplitude 5 cm has a maximum speed of 31.4 cm/s. Its time period is
questions.explanation: v_max = ωA → ω = 31.4/5 = 6.28 rad/s = 2π, so T = 2π/ω = 1 s.

questions.question: The time taken by a particle in SHM to move from the mean position to half the amplitude is
questions.explanation: x = A sin(ωt) = A/2 → ωt = π/6 → t = (π/6)/(2π/T) = T/12. Mean to full amplitude takes T/4.

questions.question: A particle of mass 0.2 kg oscillates with amplitude 0.05 m and time period π/2 s. Its total energy is
A simple pendulum is inside a lift accelerating upwards with acceleration a. Its time period is
questions.explanation: The effective gravity in the accelerating frame is g_eff = g + a, so T = 2π√(l/(g+a)) — the pendulum runs faster. In free fall (a = g downwards) it stops swinging altogether.

questions.question: Two springs of constants k₁ = 300 N/m and k₂ = 600 N/m are connected in parallel to a 4 kg block. The frequency of oscillation is about
questions.explanation: Parallel springs add: k_eff = 900 N/m. ω = √(k/m) = √225 = 15 rad/s, f = ω/2π ≈ 2.4 Hz.

questions.question: A uniform rod of length L hangs from one end and oscillates as a physical pendulum. Its time period is
questions.explanation: I = mL²/3 about the end, distance of COM d = L/2, so T = 2π√(I/mgd) = 2π√((L²/3)/(gL/2)) = 2π√(2L/3g).

Solved examples + exercises.

quests.title: D+1 · Lock-in
quests.description: Redo 5 cold mistakes + state the wave card aloud. 15 min.

questions.question: The speed of a transverse wave on a stretched string depends on
options: the tension and the linear mass density of the string
the tension and the frequency of the wave
the length and the mass of the string only
questions.explanation: v = √(T/μ). Frequency and amplitude do not appear — changing the frequency changes λ, not v.

questions.question: Two tuning forks of frequencies 256 Hz and 260 Hz are sounded together. The number of beats heard per second is
questions.explanation: Beat frequency = |f₁ − f₂| = 4 Hz, i.e. 4 loudness maxima per second.

questions.question: In a standing wave, the distance between two consecutive nodes is
questions.explanation: Nodes repeat every half wavelength, exactly like the loop pattern on a plucked guitar string.

questions.question: Which harmonics are present in an organ pipe closed at one end?
questions.explanation: A closed end must be a node and the open end an antinode, which allows only λ/4, 3λ/4, 5λ/4 … — the odd harmonics. An open pipe allows all of them.

questions.question: The sound of a source moving towards a stationary observer appears
options: of higher frequency than the true frequency
of the same frequency but louder
of the same frequency but softer
questions.explanation: The wavefronts get compressed ahead of the source, so more crests arrive per second: f′ = fv/(v − v_s). The pitch rises (train whistle effect).

questions.question: The distance between a node and the next antinode in a stationary wave is
questions.explanation: Amplitude varies as sin(kx): zero at nodes, maximum a quarter wavelength away. Node to node is λ/2, node to antinode λ/4.

questions.question: An echo is heard 0.8 s after a clap, from a wall 132 m away. The speed of sound is
questions.explanation: The sound travels there and back: v = 2d/t = 264/0.8 = 330 m/s — a nice round number, which is why exam numbers like this are chosen.

questions.question: In a stationary wave, the energy
options: is not transported — it is localised between the nodes
questions.explanation: A stationary wave is the superposition of two identical waves travelling opposite ways; the net energy flux is zero, though energy sloshes between KE and PE within each loop.

questions.question: For the wave y = 0.05 sin π(4t − 0.02x), with x in metre and t in second, the wave speed is
questions.explanation: Compare with y = A sin(ωt − kx): ω = 4π, k = 0.02π, so v = ω/k = 4π/0.02π = 200 m/s. Note λ = 2π/k = 100 m.

questions.question: A string of linear density 0.01 kg/m is under a tension of 100 N. The speed of a transverse wave and the fundamental frequency of a 1 m length are
questions.explanation: v = √(100/0.01) = 100 m/s. For a string fixed at both ends f₁ = v/2L = 100/2 = 50 Hz.

questions.question: A closed organ pipe of length 0.5 m resonates at its fundamental. If v = 340 m/s, the frequency is
questions.explanation: Closed pipe: f₁ = v/4L = 340/2 = 170 Hz. An open pipe of the same length would give 340 Hz — exactly double.

questions.question: A source of 500 Hz approaches a stationary listener at 34 m/s (v = 340 m/s). The apparent frequency is about
questions.explanation: f′ = f v/(v − v_s) = 500 × 340/306 = 555.6 Hz. Rounding to 556 Hz is closer than 550 — always carry the division through.

questions.question: A tuning fork gives 5 beats/s with a 512 Hz fork. On loading the unknown fork with wax the beats fall to 2. Its true frequency is
questions.explanation: Loading lowers the fork's frequency. Beats dropping from 5 to 2 means the unknown was approaching 512 from above — so it was 517 Hz (507 would have moved further away and increased the beats).

questions.question: A closed pipe resonates at 340 Hz and the next higher resonance is at 1020 Hz. The fundamental frequency is
questions.explanation: In a closed pipe resonances occur at odd multiples: 340 (1st), 1020 (3rd). The fundamental is the lowest, 340 Hz — there is no resonance between them.

questions.question: Two waves of amplitudes 3 and 4 units and the same frequency travel in the same direction with a phase difference of π/2. The resultant amplitude is
questions.explanation: A = √(3² + 4² + 2·3·4·cos 90°) = √25 = 5 units. A phase difference of π/2 makes the cross term vanish — a 3-4-5 triangle.

questions.question: The stationary wave y = 4 sin(πx/3) cos(40πt) has nodes separated by
questions.explanation: sin(πx/3) = 0 at x = 0, 3, 6, 9 … so consecutive nodes are 3 m apart = λ/2, giving λ = 6 m (check: k = π/3 → λ = 6 m).

Solved examples + exercises.

quests.description: Electric flux, Gauss's law, field of an infinitely long straight charged wire, an infinite plane sheet and a uniformly charged thin spherical shell (inside and outside), field inside a conductor, behaviour of conductors in electrostatic equilibrium. Exercises closed book.

quests.description: State Coulomb's law with the 1/4πε₀ value · the three standard Gauss results (line λ/2πε₀r, sheet σ/2ε₀, conductor σ/ε₀) · dipole fields 2kp/r³ (axial) and kp/r³ (equatorial) · why the field inside a charged conductor is zero · ≥80% NCERT exercises unaided.
