quests.title: D+1 · Lock-in
quests.description: Redo 5 cold mistakes + state the electrostatics card aloud. 15 min.

questions.question: The charge on an electron is 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. The number of electrons that make up a charge of −1 C is about
questions.explanation: n = Q/e = 1/1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 6.25 × 10¹⁸. This is a favourite NEET one-liner.

questions.question: If the distance between two point charges is doubled, the Coulomb force between them becomes
questions.explanation: F ∝ 1/r². Doubling r reduces the force to 1/4 — an inverse-square law, like gravitation.

questions.question: The electric field inside a charged conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is
options: proportional to the distance from the centre
questions.explanation: Free charges on a conductor rearrange until the interior field cancels. The charges end up entirely on the outer surface.

questions.question: The electric field at a point on the equatorial line of a short electric dipole varies with distance r as
questions.explanation: Equatorial field kp/r³, axial field 2kp/r³ — both fall faster than a point charge's 1/r², and the axial field is exactly twice the equatorial one at the same distance.

questions.question: Electric field lines
options: start on positive charges and end on negative charges
form closed loops in all cases
start on negative charges and end on positive charges
questions.explanation: Field lines begin on + and end on − (or go to infinity); they never cross, because the field has a single definite direction at every point.

questions.question: The torque on a dipole of moment p in a uniform field E, when p makes an angle θ with E, is
questions.explanation: τ = pE sinθ — zero when the dipole lies along the field (θ = 0) and maximum when it is perpendicular (θ = 90°).

questions.question: The electric field due to an infinite plane sheet of charge density σ is
questions.explanation: A sheet gives a uniform field σ/2ε₀ on both sides at every distance. Interestingly, the field of a charged conductor surface is twice that, σ/ε₀.

questions.question: Charge on a body is always an integral multiple of e. This is called
questions.explanation: q = ne with n an integer. Charge is also conserved in every process — the two ideas are different and NEET loves testing which is which.

questions.question: Two point charges of 1 μC each are placed 1 m apart in vacuum. The force between them is
questions.explanation: F = kq₁q₂/r² = 9 × 10⁹ × (10⁻⁶)²/1² = 9 × 10⁻³ N — repulsive, since both are positive.

questions.question: An electric dipole of moment 4 × 10⁻⁹ C·m is held at 30° to a uniform field of 5 × 10⁴ N/C. The torque on it is
A closed surface encloses a charge of 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C. The total electric flux through the surface is (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² SI)
questions.explanation: Φ = q/ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹²/8.85 × 10⁻¹² = 1 N·m²/C. Flux depends only on the enclosed charge, never on the shape.

questions.question: Two positive charges of 9e and e are 16 cm apart. The point between them where the field is zero lies at a distance from the smaller charge of
questions.explanation: Set 9e/(16 − x)² = e/x² → 3/(16 − x) = 1/x → x = 4 cm from the small charge (and 12 cm from the big one) — the null point always sits nearer the smaller charge.

questions.question: An electron is placed in a uniform field of 10⁴ N/C. Its acceleration is about
questions.explanation: a = eE/m = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 10⁴)/(9.1 × 10⁻³¹) ≈ 1.76 × 10¹⁵ m/s² — enormous because the electron mass is tiny.

questions.question: A dipole placed in a uniform field has zero potential energy when
questions.explanation: U = −pE cosθ, minimum (−pE) at θ = 0 and zero at θ = 90°. The stable equilibrium is p parallel to E.

questions.question: A uniform field of 100 N/C passes normally through a flat area of 10 m². The flux through it is
questions.explanation: Φ = EA cosθ = 100 × 10 × 1 = 1000 N·m²/C, since the field is along the normal (cos 0° = 1).

questions.question: The electric field at the centre of a uniformly charged ring of radius R is
questions.explanation: At the centre every element's field is cancelled by the diametrically opposite element. On the axis the field is maximum at a distance R/√2 from the centre.

quests.description: Electric potential and potential difference, V = kq/r for a point charge, potential due to a system of charges and a dipole, equipotential surfaces, relation between E and V (E = −dV/dr), potential energy of a system of charges and of a dipole in a field. Solved examples + exercises.

quests.title: D+1 · Lock-in
quests.description: Redo 5 cold mistakes + state the capacitor card aloud. 15 min.

questions.question: The work done in moving a charge from one point to another on an equipotential surface is
questions.explanation: W = q(V₂ − V₁) and on an equipotential V₂ = V₁, so W = 0. That is precisely what defines an equipotential surface.

questions.question: The potential at the midpoint between two equal positive charges q separated by 2d is
questions.explanation: Potential is a scalar: add kq/d + kq/d = 2kq/d. The FIELD there is zero, but the potential is not — a very common trap.

questions.question: Three capacitors of 3 μF each are connected in series. The equivalent capacitance is
questions.explanation: Series: 1/C = 3 × (1/3) = 1 → C = 1 μF = C₀/n. Series always gives less than the smallest capacitor.

questions.question: Two capacitors of equal capacitance, one charged and the other uncharged, are connected together. The fraction of the stored energy lost as heat is
questions.explanation: Final energy is half the initial energy: ½(2C)(V/2)² vs ½CV². The other half goes into heat in the wires — irrespective of the resistance.

questions.question: A capacitor of 2 μF is charged to 100 V. The charge and energy stored are
A dielectric slab of constant K is inserted between the plates of a charged capacitor that is disconnected from the battery. Which quantity stays unchanged?
options: the electric field between the plates
questions.explanation: With the battery out of the circuit, no charge can flow: Q is fixed. Then C → KC, so V = Q/C falls K times and the energy ½Q²/C also falls.

questions.question: The unit of capacitance, the farad, equals
questions.explanation: C = Q/V so 1 F = 1 C/V. The same relation gives V = J/C — don't mix up the two.

questions.question: The potential at any point inside a hollow charged spherical conductor is
options: equal to kQ/r at each interior point
constant everywhere and equal to that at the surface
questions.explanation: With E = 0 inside, moving a test charge needs no work, so V is uniform inside and equal to kQ/R at the surface.

questions.question: A parallel-plate capacitor has plate area A and separation d. If both A and d are doubled, the capacitance
questions.explanation: C = ε₀A/d: A doubles and d doubles, so C is unchanged. Capacitance cares about the ratio, not the absolute size.

questions.question: A 6 μF and a 3 μF capacitor are in series across a 6 V battery. The charge on each capacitor is
questions.explanation: C_eq = (6 × 3)/9 = 2 μF, Q = CV = 12 μC. In series each capacitor carries the SAME charge but different voltages (2 V and 4 V here).

questions.question: The capacitance of an isolated sphere of radius 9 m is about
questions.explanation: C = 4πε₀R = R/9 × 10⁹ = 9/9 × 10⁹ = 10⁻⁹ F = 1 nF. Earth itself has a capacitance of only about 711 μF.

questions.question: A 1 μF capacitor charged to 100 V is joined to an uncharged 3 μF capacitor. The common potential difference is
questions.explanation: Charge is conserved: 100 μC shared over 4 μF gives V = 25 V. Only 12.5 μJ survives out of the initial 50 μJ.

questions.question: A charge of 2 μC is moved between two points whose potentials differ by 20 V. The work done is
questions.explanation: W = qΔV = 2 × 10⁻⁶ × 20 = 4 × 10⁻⁵ J = 40 μJ. Whether the charge is positive or negative changes only the sign.

questions.question: A 5 μF capacitor is charged to 200 V. The energy stored is
questions.explanation: E = ½CV² = 0.5 × 5 × 10⁻⁶ × 4 × 10⁴ = 0.1 J. Watch the 10⁻⁶ — the units are where everyone slips.

questions.question: The potential at 0.5 m from a charge of 4 μC is
questions.explanation: V = kq/r = 9 × 10⁹ × 4 × 10⁻⁶/0.5 = 7.2 × 10⁴ V. Potential falls as 1/r, unlike the field's 1/r².

questions.question: A capacitor C charged to V is connected to an identical uncharged capacitor. The final total energy of the system is
questions.explanation: Initial energy ½CV²; the shared charge CV sits at the common potential V/2 across 2C, giving ½(2C)(V/2)² = ¼CV². Half the energy is dissipated — this is true for ANY value of connecting resistance.

quests.description: Redo 5 cold mistakes + state the current card aloud. 15 min.

questions.question: A wire carries a steady current of 1 A. The number of electrons crossing any section per second is about
questions.explanation: I = q/t → q = 1 C per second; n = 1/1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 6.25 × 10¹⁸. Compare this huge number with the drift speed, which is under a millimetre per second.

questions.question: The drift velocity of free electrons in a metallic conductor carrying a normal current is of the order of
questions.explanation: Around 0.1 mm/s — yet the current appears instantly because the electric field that starts the motion travels at nearly the speed of light.

questions.question: Which pair of materials is used for making standard resistance coils?
options: Manganin and constantan — high resistivity, low temperature coefficient
questions.explanation: Standard resistors need resistance that barely changes with temperature, so alloys with a very small temperature coefficient are chosen.

questions.question: If a copper wire is stretched to twice its length (volume constant), its resistance becomes
questions.explanation: Stretching to 2L halves the area. R = ρL/A → (2)/(1/2) = 4 times. Both length and area work against you.

questions.question: In a parallel combination of resistors, the equivalent resistance is
options: less than the smallest resistance in the combination
equal to the average of the resistances
questions.explanation: Adding a parallel path always adds a new route for current, so R_eq < R_min. In series it is the opposite: R_eq > R_max.

questions.question: The terminal voltage of a cell of emf ε and internal resistance r when it delivers current I is
questions.explanation: The cell's own resistance eats part of its emf: V = ε − Ir. A cell being CHARGED (current driven in) shows V = ε + Ir instead.

questions.question: Kirchhoff's junction rule is a statement of the conservation of
questions.explanation: Charge in = charge out at a junction (ΣI = 0). The loop rule is the one that states conservation of energy.

questions.question: The commercial unit of electrical energy, 1 kWh, equals
questions.explanation: 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. This is the unit your electricity bill uses.

questions.question: A 6 Ω and a 3 Ω resistor are joined in parallel across a 6 V battery of negligible internal resistance. The current through the 6 Ω resistor is
questions.explanation: In parallel each resistor sees the full 6 V: I = 6/6 = 1 A through the 6 Ω, and 2 A through the 3 Ω (total 3 A).

questions.question: A potentiometer wire 10 m long has a potential gradient of 0.2 V/m. A cell balances at 40 cm. The emf of the cell is
questions.explanation: V = k × l = 0.2 × 0.4 = 0.08 V. The potentiometer is a null method — it draws no current from the cell, so it measures the true emf.

questions.question: In a balanced Wheatstone bridge P = 4 Ω, Q = 8 Ω, R = 6 Ω. The unknown S is
questions.explanation: Balance: P/Q = R/S → 4/8 = 6/S → S = 12 Ω. At balance no current flows through the galvanometer, whatever its resistance.

questions.question: A cell of emf 2 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω is connected to 1.5 Ω. The terminal voltage is
questions.explanation: I = 2/2 = 1 A; V = ε − Ir = 2 − 0.5 = 1.5 V. Exactly 0.5 V is 'lost' inside the cell.

questions.question: An electric bulb is rated 100 W, 220 V. Its resistance is about
questions.explanation: R = V²/P = 220²/100 = 484 Ω. At the operating temperature the filament resistance is much higher than its cold value.

questions.question: A current of 1 A flows through a copper wire of cross-section 10⁻⁶ m² with n = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³. The drift speed is about
questions.explanation: v_d = I/(neA) = 1/(8.5 × 10²⁸ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 10⁻⁶) ≈ 7.4 × 10⁻⁵ m/s — a slow collective crawl that still lights the bulb instantly.

questions.question: Three equal resistors dissipate a total power H when connected in series across a supply. Connected in parallel across the same supply they dissipate
questions.explanation: Series: R_eq = 3R, P = V²/3R. Parallel: R_eq = R/3, P = 3V²/R. Ratio = 9. For n resistors the ratio is n².

questions.question: For maximum power transfer from a cell of emf ε and internal resistance r to an external resistance R,
options: R must be much greater than r
R must be much less than r
questions.explanation: P_ext = ε²R/(R + r)² is maximum at R = r, where the cell delivers efficiency of exactly 50%. High efficiency and high power are different goals.

quests.description: Redo 5 cold mistakes + state the magnetism card aloud. 15 min.

questions.question: The magnetic field at the centre of a circular loop of radius R carrying current I is
questions.explanation: B = μ₀I/2R, directed perpendicular to the plane by the right-hand rule. For N turns it becomes μ₀NI/2R.

questions.question: The magnetic force on a charged particle moving in a magnetic field is zero when
options: the velocity is perpendicular to the field
the velocity is parallel or antiparallel to the field
questions.explanation: F = qvB sinθ = 0 when θ = 0 or 180°. That is why a particle moving along B is undeflected and plots a straight line.

questions.question: A charged particle of mass m and charge q moves perpendicular to a uniform field B. The radius of its circular path is
questions.explanation: The magnetic force supplies the centripetal force: qvB = mv²/r → r = mv/qB. Faster or heavier particles swing wider circles.

questions.question: The time period of revolution of a charged particle in a uniform magnetic field is
options: independent of its speed and radius
questions.explanation: T = 2πm/qB contains no v or r — this is the key to the cyclotron: faster particles take bigger circles but the same time.

questions.question: The magnetic field inside a long solenoid carrying current I with n turns per metre is
questions.explanation: B = μ₀nI uniformly inside, and nearly zero outside. That is why solenoids are the standard way to make a uniform field.

questions.question: A galvanometer is converted into an ammeter by connecting
options: a high resistance in series with it
a low resistance shunt in parallel with it
questions.explanation: The shunt diverts most of the current around the coil, so the instrument can handle large currents. A voltmeter is made with a high resistance in SERIES instead.

questions.question: A cyclotron's oscillator frequency depends on the charge and mass of the particle and on the magnetic field as
questions.explanation: f = qB/2πm, independent of the particle's speed and of the dee radius. That constancy is exactly what lets one oscillator keep accelerating the particle.

questions.question: Two long parallel wires carrying currents in the same direction
questions.explanation: Parallel currents attract, antiparallel repel. This is also the basis of the ampere, defined through the force per unit length.

questions.question: Two long parallel wires 0.1 m apart each carry 5 A in the same direction. The force per metre on each wire is
questions.explanation: F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/2πd = (2 × 10⁻⁷ × 25)/0.1 = 5 × 10⁻⁵ N/m, attractive because the currents are parallel.

questions.question: A proton moves at 2 × 10⁶ m/s perpendicular to a 0.5 T field. The radius of its path is about (m_p = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg)
A coil of 100 turns and area 0.01 m² carries 1 A in a field of 0.1 T, with its plane parallel to the field. The torque on the coil is
questions.explanation: Plane parallel to B means the normal is perpendicular to B, θ = 90°: τ = NIAB = 100 × 1 × 0.01 × 0.1 = 0.1 N·m, the maximum torque.

questions.question: A galvanometer of resistance 100 Ω gives full-scale deflection for 1 mA. To convert it into an ammeter of range 10 A, the shunt needed is about
questions.explanation: S = I_gG/(I − I_g) ≈ (10⁻³ × 100)/10 = 0.01 Ω. A very small shunt — the ammeter must have negligible resistance.

questions.question: The same galvanometer (G = 100 Ω, I_g = 1 mA) is converted into a voltmeter of range 10 V by connecting
questions.explanation: R = V/I_g − G = 10/10⁻³ − 100 = 9900 Ω in series. High resistance in series is what makes the voltmeter draw almost no current.

questions.question: A circular coil of 100 turns and radius 10 cm carries 1 A. The field at its centre is about
questions.explanation: B = μ₀NI/2R = (4π × 10⁻⁷ × 100 × 1)/(0.2) ≈ 6.3 × 10⁻⁴ T. Notice how much stronger a coil is than a straight wire.

questions.question: The maximum kinetic energy a cyclotron of dee radius R can give a particle of charge q and mass m in field B is
questions.explanation: The particle exits at r = R with K = ½mv² and v = qBR/m, giving K = q²B²R²/2m. Energy grows as the square of B and R.

questions.question: The current sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer can be increased by
options: increasing the torsion constant of the suspension
decreasing the area of the coil
increasing the number of turns and the magnetic field
questions.explanation: Sensitivity = NAB/k. More turns and a stronger field mean more deflection for the same current; a stiffer suspension reduces it.

quests.description: Redo 5 cold mistakes + state the magnetism card aloud. 15 min.

questions.question: The angle of dip at the magnetic equator of the earth is
questions.explanation: At the magnetic equator the earth's field is entirely horizontal, so the dip is zero. At the magnetic poles the dip is 90°.

questions.question: The magnetic susceptibility of a diamagnetic substance is
questions.explanation: Diamagnets are weakly repelled by a magnet: χ is small and negative (−1 ≤ χ < 0). Superconductors reach the extreme χ = −1.

questions.question: A ferromagnetic substance is heated above its Curie temperature. It becomes
questions.explanation: Above T_C thermal agitation destroys the domain alignment, and the material behaves as a paramagnet: χ ∝ 1/T (Curie's law).

questions.question: The horizontal component of the earth's field is B_H. If the angle of dip at a place is δ, then B_H equals
questions.explanation: The total field B splits into B_H = B cos δ (horizontal) and B_V = B sin δ (vertical), so B_H/B_V = cot δ.

questions.question: The magnetic field lines of a bar magnet
options: form closed continuous loops from the N pole to the S pole outside and inside the magnet
start at the N pole and end at the S pole
start at the S pole and end at the N pole
cross each other near the poles
questions.explanation: Magnetic field lines never begin or end — there are no magnetic monopoles. Outside the magnet they run N to S; inside, S to N.

questions.question: The material best suited for the core of an electromagnet is
options: soft iron — high permeability, low coercivity
questions.explanation: An electromagnet must lose its magnetism the instant the current stops, so it needs a low coercivity and narrow hysteresis loop: soft iron.

questions.question: The magnetic moment of a bar magnet of pole strength m and length 2l is
options: m × 2l, directed from N to S
m × 2l, directed from S to N
questions.explanation: M = m(2l), a vector pointing from the south to the north pole — that is inside the magnet, opposite to the external field lines.

questions.question: The time period of a bar magnet oscillating in the earth's horizontal field is T. If its magnetic moment M is halved, the period becomes
questions.explanation: T = 2π√(I/MB_H) ∝ 1/√M. Halving M multiplies the period by √2 — this is exactly how a vibration magnetometer compares moments.

questions.question: A bar magnet of moment 2 A·m² is placed in a field of 0.5 T at 30° to it. The torque on it is
questions.explanation: τ = MB sinθ = 2 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.5 N·m. Its potential energy at that angle is U = −MB cos30° = −0.87 J.

questions.question: A material has magnetic susceptibility χ = 599. Its relative permeability is
questions.explanation: μ_r = 1 + χ = 600. For diamagnets μ_r is slightly less than 1; for ferromagnets it can run into thousands.

questions.question: At a place the earth's total field is 0.5 G and the dip is 60°. The horizontal component is
questions.explanation: B_H = B cos 60° = 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25 G. The vertical component would be B sin60° ≈ 0.43 G.

questions.question: The area enclosed by a hysteresis loop represents
options: the energy dissipated as heat per unit volume per cycle
questions.explanation: Each cycle costs energy equal to the loop area times the volume. Transformer cores need narrow loops precisely to keep this loss small.

questions.question: The magnetic field on the axial line of a short bar magnet of moment M at distance r is
questions.explanation: Axial: μ₀2M/4πr³, exactly twice the equatorial value μ₀M/4πr³ at the same distance. Both fall as 1/r³, much faster than a current's 1/r.

questions.question: The time period of a magnet oscillating in a field doubles. Its magnetic moment must have become
questions.explanation: T ∝ 1/√M, so T doubling needs M to fall by a factor of 4. Check: T = 2π√(I/MB).

questions.question: A substance has μ_r = 0.9999. The substance is
questions.explanation: μ_r slightly less than 1 means χ = μ_r − 1 is small and negative — the defining signature of a diamagnetic material such as bismuth or water.

questions.question: Two identical short bar magnets are placed perpendicular to each other with their centres coincident. The resultant magnetic moment of the combination is
questions.explanation: Two perpendicular vectors of magnitude M add to √(M² + M²) = √2 M. Vector addition applies to magnetic moments exactly as it does to forces.

quests.title: D+1 · Lock-in
quests.description: Redo 5 cold mistakes + state the EMI card aloud. 15 min.

questions.question: Lenz's law is a consequence of the conservation of
questions.explanation: The induced current opposes the change that produced it — otherwise you could get electrical energy for free, which would violate energy conservation.

questions.question: The magnitude of the induced emf in a coil is
options: directly proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux
questions.explanation: ε = −dΦ/dt. A steady flux, however large, induces nothing; only a CHANGING flux does.

questions.question: A conducting rod of length L moves with velocity v perpendicular to a field B, with v ⊥ L. The emf induced across it is
questions.explanation: The free charges in the rod are pushed by qvB and separate until the electric force balances it: ε = BLv. This is the generator in its simplest form.

questions.question: The SI unit of self-inductance, the henry, is equal to
questions.explanation: ε = −L dI/dt, so 1 H = 1 V·s/A = 1 Wb/A. It is a measure of 'electrical inertia' against current change.

questions.question: The energy stored in an inductor of inductance L carrying current I is
questions.explanation: U = ½LI², the exact magnetic analogue of ½CV² for a capacitor. It lives in the magnetic field, just as capacitor energy lives in the electric field.

questions.question: Eddy currents are used in
questions.explanation: Eddy currents heat metal (induction furnace, induction cooking) and damp motion (dead-beat galvanometer). In transformer cores they are a nuisance, so cores are laminated.

questions.question: In a coil the magnetic flux is constant with time. The induced emf is
questions.explanation: ε ∝ dΦ/dt, so a static flux gives no emf — the same reason a stationary magnet near a coil produces no current.

questions.question: Mutual inductance of two coils depends on
options: only the resistance of the coils
the frequency of the source only
the geometry of the coils, their separation and their relative orientation
questions.explanation: M is purely geometric plus the medium: M = k√(L₁L₂). The currents do not change M, they only set the induced emf M dI/dt.

questions.question: A coil of 100 turns and area 0.01 m² lies perpendicular to a field that changes at 0.5 T/s. The induced emf is
questions.explanation: ε = NA dB/dt = 100 × 0.01 × 0.5 = 0.5 V. The area and turn count amplify the flux change.

questions.question: A 1 m rod moves at 10 m/s perpendicular to a 0.5 T field. The emf across it is
questions.explanation: ε = Blv = 0.5 × 1 × 10 = 5 V. In a closed circuit the induced current would be ε/R.

questions.question: A coil of resistance 10 Ω has its flux changed by 0.05 Wb. The charge that flows is
questions.explanation: q = ΔΦ/R = 0.05/10 = 5 × 10⁻³ C. Notice the charge does not depend on how fast the change happened.

questions.question: A rod of length 0.5 m rotates at 10 rad/s about one end in a field of 0.2 T (field ⊥ plane of rotation). The emf induced between its ends is
questions.explanation: ε = ½BωL² = 0.5 × 0.2 × 10 × 0.25 = 0.25 V. The factor ½ comes from averaging v = ωx over the length.

questions.question: An inductor of 2 H carries a current of 3 A. The energy stored is
questions.explanation: U = ½LI² = 0.5 × 2 × 9 = 9 J. Compare with a capacitor: both store energy as ½ × (constant) × (quantity)².

questions.question: A secondary coil of 0.2 H mutual inductance has its primary current changing at 2 A/s. The emf induced in the secondary is
questions.explanation: ε = M dI/dt = 0.2 × 2 = 0.4 V. Mutual inductance converts a current change in one coil into a voltage in another — the heart of the transformer.

questions.question: A solenoid of 1000 turns, length 1 m and cross-section 10⁻³ m² has a self-inductance of about
questions.explanation: L = μ₀N²A/l = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 10⁶ × 10⁻³ = 1.26 × 10⁻³ H. Long solenoids give L proportional to N² — turns matter a lot.

questions.question: A coil of 200 turns and area 0.05 m² rotates at 50 rad/s in a 0.2 T field. The peak emf is
questions.explanation: ε₀ = NBAω = 200 × 0.2 × 0.05 × 50 = 100 V. The rms emf would be 100/√2 ≈ 70.7 V.

questions.question: The domestic AC supply in India is 220 V. Its peak value is about
questions.explanation: V₀ = √2 × V_rms = 1.414 × 220 ≈ 311 V. Insulation must survive the peak — which is why appliances are rated for far more than 220 V.

questions.question: A capacitor in an AC circuit
options: leads the current over the voltage by π/2
is exactly in phase with the current
questions.explanation: Mnemonic CIVIL: in a Capacitor, I leads V (CIV); in an inductor, V leads I (VIL). So a capacitor's current is a quarter cycle ahead of its voltage.

questions.question: The average power consumed by a pure inductor or a pure capacitor over a full cycle is
questions.explanation: Voltage and current are 90° out of phase, so cos φ = 0: energy goes in and comes back each quarter cycle, with no net consumption.

questions.question: At resonance in a series LCR circuit,
options: X_L = X_C and the impedance is zero
X_L = X_C and the impedance equals R
questions.explanation: At the resonant frequency the two reactances cancel, so Z = R (minimum) and the current is maximum with a power factor of 1.

questions.question: The resonant frequency of a series LCR circuit is
questions.explanation: ω₀ = 1/√(LC). Note it does not contain R at all — the resistance only sets how SHARP the resonance is.

questions.question: A step-down transformer has
options: more turns in the primary than in the secondary
questions.explanation: V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p. Fewer secondary turns means lower secondary voltage — and correspondingly higher current in the secondary.

questions.question: A choke coil is preferred to a resistor for reducing AC current because it
options: reduces the current without dissipating much power
questions.explanation: A choke's opposition is reactive (X_L = ωL), so energy is stored and returned rather than burnt as heat — no power loss, unlike a resistor.

questions.question: The rms value of an AC current of peak value 14 A is about
questions.explanation: I_rms = I₀/√2 = 14/1.414 ≈ 9.9 ≈ 10 A. When an instrument reads 10 A on AC, the peak is really 14 A.

questions.question: A 100 Ω resistor and a 0.1 H inductor are in series across 220 V, 50 Hz. The impedance is about
questions.explanation: X_L = 2π × 50 × 0.1 ≈ 31.4 Ω, so Z = √(100² + 31.4²) ≈ 105 Ω. Phasors add in quadrature, never directly.

questions.question: An inductor of 1 H and a capacitor of 1 μF form a series circuit. The resonant frequency is about
questions.explanation: f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)) = 1/(2π × 10⁻³) ≈ 159 Hz. Large L and small C still give an audible-range resonance.

questions.question: An AC circuit has V_rms = 220 V, I_rms = 2 A and a power factor of 0.5. The average power is
questions.explanation: P = VI cos φ = 220 × 2 × 0.5 = 220 W. Half the product VI is 'wattless' — it sloshes back and forth.

questions.question: A transformer with a turns ratio 10 : 1 is fed 220 V. If the secondary supplies 10 A, the primary current (ideal) is
questions.explanation: Ideal transformer: V_pI_p = V_sI_s → 220 × I_p = 22 × 10 → I_p = 1 A. Voltage steps down by 10, current steps up by 10.

questions.question: The reactance of a 1 μF capacitor at 50 Hz is about
questions.explanation: X_C = 1/(2πfC) = 1/(2π × 50 × 10⁻⁶) ≈ 3183 Ω ≈ 3.2 kΩ. Capacitors block DC but pass high frequencies easily.

questions.question: A series LCR circuit has R = 30 Ω, X_L = 50 Ω and X_C = 10 Ω, connected to 200 V (rms). The rms current is
questions.explanation: Z = √(30² + 40²) = 50 Ω, so I = 200/50 = 4 A. The net reactance is the DIFFERENCE of X_L and X_C, not the sum.

questions.question: In a series LCR circuit R = 10 Ω, L = 0.1 H and ω₀ = 1000 rad/s. The Q factor is
questions.explanation: Q = ω₀L/R = (1000 × 0.1)/10 = 10. A higher Q means a sharper resonance peak and a more selective circuit.

questions.question: The frequency of oscillation of a charge in an ideal LC circuit with L = 1 mH and C = 1 μF is about
questions.explanation: f = 1/(2π√(LC)) = 1/(2π√(10⁻⁹)) ≈ 5033 Hz ≈ 5 kHz. Energy swings between the capacitor's electric field and the inductor's magnetic field.

questions.question: The displacement current inside a charging parallel-plate capacitor is
options: ε₀ times the rate of change of electric flux
equal to the conduction current only at the plates
μ₀ times the rate of change of magnetic flux
questions.explanation: I_D = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt. Between the plates there is no conduction current, yet the circuit current is continuous — this is exactly the gap Maxwell's term fills.

questions.question: In an electromagnetic wave, the electric and magnetic fields are
options: mutually perpendicular and both perpendicular to the direction of propagation
parallel to the direction of propagation
90° out of phase with each other
questions.explanation: EM waves are transverse: E ⊥ B ⊥ direction of travel, and E and B oscillate in phase (they peak together).

questions.question: The speed of an electromagnetic wave in vacuum is given by
questions.explanation: c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s. That this falls out of purely electrical and magnetic constants was Maxwell's greatest triumph.

questions.question: Which of the following has the shortest wavelength?
questions.explanation: Order of increasing wavelength: gamma < X-ray < UV < visible < infrared < microwave < radio. Gamma rays have wavelengths below 10⁻¹⁰ m.

questions.question: The ratio of the electric field amplitude to the magnetic field amplitude in an EM wave in vacuum is
questions.explanation: E₀/B₀ = c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s. So if you know one amplitude, the other follows immediately.

questions.question: Which radiation is used in remote controls of television sets?
questions.explanation: Infrared (roughly 700 nm to 1 mm) is emitted by warm objects, is easily produced by LEDs and is harmless at low intensity — perfect for remote controls.

questions.question: Electromagnetic waves carry
questions.explanation: A photon-like momentum p = U/c means an EM wave exerts radiation pressure — the basis of the solar sail and of the tails of comets pointing away from the Sun.

questions.question: The frequency of an EM wave of wavelength 3 cm is
questions.explanation: f = c/λ = (3 × 10⁸)/(3 × 10⁻²) = 10¹⁰ Hz = 10 GHz — the microwave band used by radar and satellite links.

questions.question: The electric field amplitude of an EM wave in vacuum is 60 V/m. The magnetic field amplitude is
questions.explanation: B₀ = E₀/c = 60/(3 × 10⁸) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ T. Magnetic amplitudes look tiny but produce exactly matching energy density.

questions.question: The intensity of an EM wave of electric amplitude 30 V/m in vacuum is about
questions.explanation: I = ½ε₀E₀²c = 0.5 × 8.85 × 10⁻¹² × 900 × 3 × 10⁸ ≈ 1.19 W/m². Halve it if you forget the ½ for the average.

questions.question: For a plane EM wave in vacuum, the average energy density stored in the electric field and that in the magnetic field are
questions.explanation: u_E = ¼ε₀E₀² and u_B = B₀²/4μ₀ are equal, thanks to E₀ = cB₀. The total average energy density is ½ε₀E₀².

questions.question: The direction of propagation of an EM wave in which E is along +x and B is along +y is
questions.explanation: The propagation direction is along E × B = x̂ × ŷ = ẑ. If you reverse either field, the wave travels the opposite way.

questions.question: Radiation falls normally on a perfectly reflecting surface of area 1 m² with intensity 3 W/m². The force on the surface is
questions.explanation: For reflection the pressure is 2I/c = 6/(3 × 10⁸) = 2 × 10⁻⁸ N/m², so the force on 1 m² is 2 × 10⁻⁸ N. Absorption would give only half this.

questions.question: X-rays are produced by
options: excitation of atoms in a discharge tube only
rapid deceleration of electrons striking a metal target
questions.explanation: X-rays come from the braking (and inner-shell transitions) of fast electrons hitting a heavy target. Gamma rays are the ones that come from nuclei.

questions.question: A plane EM wave has E₀ = 120 V/m. The average energy density of the wave is about
questions.explanation: u_avg = ½ε₀E₀² = 0.5 × 8.85 × 10⁻¹² × 14400 ≈ 6.4 × 10⁻⁸ J/m³. Multiply by c to get the intensity.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an electromagnetic wave?
questions.explanation: Ultrasound is a mechanical (pressure) wave in matter and needs a medium — it cannot travel through vacuum. All EM waves can.

questions.question: A concave mirror has a radius of curvature of 40 cm. Its focal length is
questions.explanation: f = R/2 = 20 cm for a spherical mirror — true for both concave and convex, with the sign following the convention.

questions.question: Total internal reflection can take place when light travels
options: from a rarer to a denser medium
from a denser to a rarer medium with the angle of incidence greater than the critical angle
from a denser to a rarer medium at any angle
along the normal to a surface
questions.explanation: Both conditions are needed: denser → rarer AND i > C. That is why a light ray inside water can bounce off the surface but a ray in air cannot.

questions.question: The critical angle for glass of refractive index 1.5 is about
questions.explanation: sin C = 1/n = 1/1.5 = 0.667 → C ≈ 41.8° ≈ 42°. Diamonds (n = 2.42) have C ≈ 24°, which is why they sparkle so brilliantly.

questions.question: A convex lens of focal length 50 cm has a power of
questions.explanation: P = 1/f with f in metres: 1/0.5 = +2 dioptre. A converging (convex) lens has positive power; a diverging lens has negative power.

questions.question: In a prism at minimum deviation, the angle of incidence equals the angle of emergence and
options: the refracted ray inside is parallel to the base
the ray is totally internally reflected
the prism behaves like a slab of zero thickness
questions.explanation: At minimum deviation the path is symmetric: i = e = (A + δm)/2 and the ray inside travels parallel to the base.

questions.question: Myopia (short-sightedness) is corrected by using
questions.explanation: A short-sighted eye converges too strongly, so a diverging (concave) lens of negative power shifts the image back onto the retina.

questions.question: In dispersion of white light by a prism, the colour deviated the most is
questions.explanation: Refractive index is largest for the shortest wavelength, so violet bends most and red least. Dispersion arises because n depends on λ.

questions.question: Optical fibres work on the principle of
questions.explanation: Light launched into the core strikes the cladding boundary above the critical angle repeatedly and stays trapped — even around bends. The cladding must have a lower refractive index.

questions.question: An object is placed 10 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. The image is
options: 30 cm behind the mirror, virtual, erect and 3 times magnified
30 cm in front of the mirror, real and inverted
15 cm in front, real and inverted
questions.explanation: With 1/v + 1/u = 1/f (u = −10, f = −15): 1/v = −1/15 + 1/10 = 1/30 → v = +30 cm (behind), m = −v/u = 3. Object inside the focus always gives a virtual, erect, magnified image.

questions.question: A swimming pool appears 3 m deep to a person looking straight down. If n_water = 4/3, the real depth is
questions.explanation: Apparent depth = real/n → real = 3 × 4/3 = 4 m. Refraction at a plane surface makes objects in water look shallower by the factor n.

questions.question: A convex lens of focal length 20 cm is combined with a concave lens of focal length 30 cm, in contact. The combination behaves as
options: a convex lens of focal length 60 cm
questions.explanation: P = 1/20 − 1/30 = 1/60 cm⁻¹ → f = +60 cm. In contact, powers add with their signs — this is how opticians build a prescription.

questions.question: A prism of angle 60° produces a minimum deviation of 30°. The angle of incidence is
questions.explanation: At minimum deviation i = (A + δm)/2 = (60 + 30)/2 = 45°. The angle of emergence equals the angle of incidence by symmetry.

questions.question: A glass slab of thickness 6 cm and refractive index 1.5 is placed over a dot. The dot appears raised by
questions.explanation: Shift = t(1 − 1/n) = 6(1 − 2/3) = 2 cm. The dot seems to be only 4 cm below the top surface.

questions.question: A telescope has an objective of focal length 100 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 2 cm. Its magnifying power for normal adjustment is
questions.explanation: M = fo/fe = 100/2 = 50. The length of the tube in normal adjustment is fo + fe = 102 cm.

questions.question: A convex lens of focal length 20 cm in air (n = 1.5) is immersed in water (n = 4/3). Its focal length in water becomes
questions.explanation: 1/f ∝ (n_lens/n_medium − 1): in air 0.5, in water 0.125 — one quarter. So the focal length becomes four times larger, 80 cm.

questions.question: A compound microscope has an objective of magnification 10 and an eyepiece of magnification 5. Its total magnification is
questions.explanation: M = mo × me = 10 × 5 = 50. The two magnifications multiply because the eyepiece magnifies the image already formed by the objective.

quests.description: Redo 5 cold mistakes + state the wave optics card aloud. 15 min.

questions.question: Two sources are said to be coherent if they
questions.explanation: A constant (usually zero) phase difference is what keeps the interference pattern steady. Two independent bulbs never give sustained interference because their phases drift randomly.

questions.question: In Young's double slit experiment, the fringe width is given by
questions.explanation: β = λD/d where D is the screen distance and d the slit separation. Larger wavelength or screen distance, or smaller slit separation, all give wider fringes.

questions.question: The central fringe in a Young's double slit pattern is
options: of half the width of the others
bright, because the path difference there is zero
questions.explanation: At the centre both waves travel equal distances, arrive in phase and reinforce — a bright fringe sits exactly at the centre.

questions.question: If the whole Young's double slit apparatus is immersed in water, the fringe width
questions.explanation: In water λ' = λ/n, so β' = β/n decreases (by 3/4 for n = 4/3). This is one of the classic confirmations that refraction is a wavelength effect.

questions.question: When a single slit is made narrower, the diffraction pattern on the screen
questions.explanation: Central maximum width = 2λD/a, so a smaller a gives a broader pattern. This inverse relation is the hallmark of diffraction.

questions.question: Which phenomenon establishes the transverse nature of light?
questions.explanation: Only transverse waves can be polarised. Interference and diffraction prove light is a wave; polarisation proves the vibrations are perpendicular to the direction of travel.

questions.question: Unpolarised light passes through a polaroid. The intensity of the emerging light becomes
questions.explanation: The polaroid transmits only the component along its axis, giving I₀/2 on average. A second polaroid at 90° then extinguishes the light completely.

questions.question: The diffraction of light demonstrates that light
questions.explanation: Bending around obstacles and forming a fringe pattern is impossible for a stream of particles — so light must be a wave.

questions.question: In a Young's experiment λ = 600 nm, D = 1 m and d = 1 mm. The fringe width is
questions.explanation: β = λD/d = (600 × 10⁻⁹ × 1)/10⁻³ = 6 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.6 mm. Keep everything in SI and the answer appears in metres.

questions.question: With β = 0.6 mm, the distance of the 5th bright fringe from the centre is
questions.explanation: y_n = nβ = 5 × 0.6 = 3 mm. Fringes are equally spaced, so counting from the centre is just multiplication.

questions.question: In Young's experiment, if the separation between the slits is doubled and the wavelength is halved, the fringe width
questions.explanation: β ∝ λ/d: λ halves, d doubles → β × (1/2)/(2) = 1/4. Two changes can compound in one question.

questions.question: Two waves of intensities I and 4I interfere. The ratio of maximum to minimum intensity is
questions.explanation: Amplitudes go as √I, i.e. 1 : 2. Then I_max/I_min = (2 + 1)²/(2 − 1)² = 9. Always convert intensities to amplitudes first.

questions.question: Light of 500 nm falls on a single slit 0.5 mm wide with the screen 1 m away. The width of the central maximum is
questions.explanation: Width = 2λD/a = 2 × 5 × 10⁻⁷ × 1/5 × 10⁻⁴ = 2 × 10⁻³ m = 2 mm. Notice how much wider diffraction fringes are than interference fringes in the earlier problem.

questions.question: Unpolarised light passes through two polaroids whose axes are at 60°. The fraction of the incident intensity transmitted is
questions.explanation: First polaroid: I₀/2. Second (Malus): (I₀/2)cos²60° = (I₀/2)(1/4) = I₀/8. Both factors must be included.

questions.question: The Brewster angle for a medium of refractive index 4/3 is about
questions.explanation: tan θp = n = 4/3 → θp ≈ 53°. At this angle the reflected light is completely polarised — which is why polaroid sunglasses cut glare off water.

questions.question: In Young's experiment, a thin transparent sheet of thickness t and refractive index n is placed over one slit. The central fringe shifts by
questions.explanation: The sheet adds an extra optical path (n − 1)t, so the whole pattern shifts by that amount translated to the screen: (n − 1)tD/d. The shift direction tells you which slit was covered.

quests.description: Redo 5 cold mistakes + state the modern physics card aloud. 15 min.

questions.question: The energy of a photon of wavelength λ is
questions.explanation: E = hν = hc/λ. Short wavelengths mean energetic photons — which is why UV and X-rays are damaging while radio waves are not.

questions.question: In the photoelectric effect, no emission takes place below a certain frequency, however intense the light. This frequency is called the
questions.explanation: ν₀ = φ₀/h. Below it, a single photon simply does not carry enough energy to free an electron, and intensity only increases the number of photons.

questions.question: Einstein's photoelectric equation is
questions.explanation: The photon energy is split between escaping the metal (φ₀) and the electron's kinetic energy. Everything in this chapter is this one equation rearranged.

questions.question: If the intensity of incident light is doubled (frequency unchanged), the photoelectric current
questions.explanation: Intensity sets the number of photons per second, hence the number of photoelectrons per second. The stopping potential stays exactly where it was.

questions.question: The stopping potential depends on
options: the frequency of the light and the metal used
the intensity of the light only
questions.explanation: eV₀ = hν − φ₀ involves only ν and φ₀. This insensitivity to intensity is the experiment's decisive blow against the classical wave picture.

questions.question: The de Broglie wavelength of a particle of mass m moving with velocity v is
questions.explanation: λ = h/p = h/mv. Heavier or faster means shorter wavelength — a cricket ball's wavelength is absurdly tiny.

questions.question: The de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through V volts is about
questions.explanation: λ = h/√(2meV) = 12.27/√V Å. For 100 V this gives 1.227 Å — comparable to atomic spacings, which is why electron diffraction works.

questions.question: Which experiment demonstrated the wave nature of electrons?
questions.explanation: Davisson and Germer diffracted electrons from a nickel crystal and got a pattern matching Bragg's law with λ = h/p — matter waves made real.

questions.question: The energy of a photon of wavelength 400 nm is about
questions.explanation: E = 1240/λ(nm) = 1240/400 = 3.1 eV. Memorise 1240 eV·nm — it converts half the numericals in this chapter into a single division.

questions.question: Light of 500 nm falls on a metal of work function 2.0 eV. The maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons is
questions.explanation: E = 1240/500 = 2.48 eV, so K_max = 2.48 − 2.0 = 0.48 eV and the stopping potential is 0.48 V.

questions.question: The threshold wavelength for a metal of work function 2.2 eV is about
questions.explanation: λ₀ = 1240/2.2 ≈ 564 nm. Light of longer wavelength — however intense — will never eject electrons from this metal.

questions.question: An electron is accelerated through 100 V. Its de Broglie wavelength is about
questions.explanation: λ = 12.27/√V = 12.27/10 ≈ 1.23 Å. X-ray-scale wavelengths — hence electron diffraction from crystals.

questions.question: An electron and a proton have the same kinetic energy. The de Broglie wavelength of
options: the electron is longer, since λ ∝ 1/√m
questions.explanation: λ = h/√(2mK) ∝ 1/√m, and the electron is about 1836 times lighter, so its wavelength is √1836 ≈ 43 times longer.

questions.question: The momentum of a photon of wavelength 500 nm is
questions.explanation: p = h/λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/5 × 10⁻⁷ ≈ 1.33 × 10⁻²⁷ kg m/s. Radiation pressure comes from this momentum.

questions.question: The work function of a metal is 1.5 eV and the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons is 2.5 eV. The wavelength of the incident light is about
questions.explanation: hν = 1.5 + 2.5 = 4.0 eV, so λ = 1240/4 = 310 nm — in the ultraviolet.

questions.question: The frequency of the incident light is doubled, the intensity unchanged. Then the saturation photocurrent
options: decreases, because fewer photons reach the metal per second
questions.explanation: Doubling ν at fixed intensity halves the photon rate (same power, each photon worth double), so about half as many electrons are emitted — but each one carries more energy.

questions.question: Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment established that
options: the entire positive charge and most of the mass is concentrated in a tiny nucleus
the atom is a uniform sphere of positive charge
questions.explanation: A few alpha particles bounced straight back, which is only possible if the positive charge sits in a very small, very dense centre. Most of the atom is empty space.

questions.question: In Bohr's model, the angular momentum of an electron in the nth orbit is
questions.explanation: L = nh/2π with n = 1, 2, 3 … This quantisation condition is the heart of Bohr's theory and it is what makes the orbits 'allowed'.

questions.question: The radius of the nth Bohr orbit of hydrogen varies as
questions.explanation: r_n = 0.53 n² Å, so the second orbit is four times the first (2.12 Å). Energy goes the other way, as −1/n².

questions.question: The energy of the electron in the ground state of hydrogen is
questions.explanation: E₁ = −13.6 eV. The negative sign means the electron is bound; 13.6 eV is exactly the ionisation energy of hydrogen.

questions.question: The Lyman series of the hydrogen spectrum lies in the
questions.explanation: Lyman: transitions ending at n = 1 (UV). Balmer ends at n = 2 (visible, Hα 656 nm), Paschen at n = 3 and beyond goes to the infrared.

questions.question: The energy required to excite a hydrogen atom from n = 1 to n = 2 is about
questions.explanation: ΔE = −3.4 − (−13.6) = 10.2 eV. This is the first excitation energy, the smallest quantum a hydrogen atom can absorb.

questions.question: The number of spectral lines emitted when a hydrogen atom de-excites from n = 4 to the ground state is
questions.explanation: All possible pairs give n(n − 1)/2 = 4 × 3/2 = 6 lines — 4→3, 4→2, 4→1, 3→2, 3→1 and 2→1.

questions.question: The ionisation energy of a hydrogen-like ion of atomic number Z is
questions.explanation: E_n = −13.6Z²/n² eV, so from the ground state you need 13.6Z² eV. For He⁺ that is 54.4 eV and for Li²⁺ 122.4 eV.

questions.question: The radius of the second Bohr orbit of hydrogen is
questions.explanation: r_n = 0.53n² Å → r₂ = 0.53 × 4 = 2.12 Å. Radius grows quickly because of the n² dependence.

questions.question: The energy of the electron in the n = 3 state of hydrogen is
questions.explanation: E₃ = −13.6/9 = −1.51 eV. Learning the ladder −13.6, −3.4, −1.51, −0.85, −0.54 eV makes most numericals one-step.

questions.question: The ionisation potential of Li²⁺ is
questions.explanation: Ionisation energy = 13.6Z² = 13.6 × 9 = 122.4 eV, so the ionisation potential is 122.4 V. Hydrogen-like ions with more protons bind far more tightly.

questions.question: The wavelength of the Hα line of the Balmer series (n = 3 → 2) is about
questions.explanation: ΔE = 3.4 − 1.51 = 1.89 eV → λ = 1240/1.89 ≈ 656 nm, the familiar red line of hydrogen. Hβ (486 nm) and Hγ (434 nm) follow.

questions.question: The speed of the electron in the ground state of hydrogen is about 2.18 × 10⁶ m/s. In the n = 2 orbit its speed is
questions.explanation: v_n ∝ 1/n, so v₂ = 2.18 × 10⁶/2 = 1.09 × 10⁶ m/s. Outer orbits are slower AND longer, so the period grows steeply with n.

questions.question: The de Broglie wavelength of the electron in the ground state of hydrogen corresponds to how many times the orbit circumference?
options: n depends on the orbit — the relation holds for every n
questions.explanation: Bohr's quantisation L = nh/2π is equivalent to 2πr_n = nλ. The orbit can fit exactly a whole number of matter wavelengths — a standing wave. For the ground state, n = 1.

questions.question: The energy released when a hydrogen atom makes a transition from n = 4 to n = 2 is about
questions.explanation: ΔE = 3.4 − 0.85 = 2.55 eV, which gives λ = 1240/2.55 ≈ 486 nm — the Hβ line of the Balmer series.

questions.question: A hydrogen atom absorbs a photon and the electron goes from n = 1 to n = 3. The energy of the absorbed photon is
questions.explanation: ΔE = 13.6 − 1.51 = 12.09 eV. A photon of exactly this energy can be absorbed; 10.2 eV would excite it only to n = 2.

questions.question: The radius of a nucleus of mass number A is proportional to
questions.explanation: R = R₀A^{1/3} with R₀ ≈ 1.2 fm. Volume then goes as A, which is exactly why nuclear density is the same for every nucleus.

questions.question: The density of nuclear matter is
options: about the same for all nuclei
questions.explanation: Mass ∝ A and volume ∝ A, so density ≈ 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg/m³ for all nuclei — the densest known form of ordinary matter.

questions.question: The energy equivalent of 1 atomic mass unit is
questions.explanation: 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c², a conversion worth memorising. Mass defects in nuclear reactions are quoted in u and answered in MeV.

questions.question: The binding energy per nucleon is maximum for
questions.explanation: The curve peaks around 8.8 MeV per nucleon near Fe-56 — the most stable nuclei. Both fission of heavy nuclei and fusion of light ones move towards this peak and release energy.

questions.question: After two half-lives, the fraction of radioactive nuclei left undecayed is
questions.explanation: N = N₀(1/2)² = N₀/4. Half-life is about probability, not about a fixed clock — any single nucleus may decay at any moment.

questions.question: In alpha decay, the atomic number of the daughter nucleus
questions.explanation: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus (A = 4, Z = 2), so the daughter loses 4 in mass number and 2 in charge — moving two places back in the periodic table.

questions.question: Gamma emission from a nucleus
questions.explanation: A gamma ray carries away only energy (and angular momentum) from an excited nucleus — no particles, so the mass number and charge stay put.

questions.question: The energy source of the Sun is
options: nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium
questions.explanation: Four protons fuse into a helium nucleus with about 26.7 MeV released per helium. At the Sun's rate this has kept it shining for billions of years.

questions.question: The binding energy per nucleon of helium-4 (mass defect 0.0304 u) is about
questions.explanation: Total BE = 0.0304 × 931.5 ≈ 28.3 MeV; per nucleon, divide by 4 → ≈ 7.1 MeV. Helium's exceptionally tight binding is why alpha particles are emitted so readily.

questions.question: A radioactive sample has a half-life of 20 minutes. The fraction remaining after one hour is
questions.explanation: 60 minutes is three half-lives, so (1/2)³ = 1/8 = 12.5% remains. Always count half-lives, never seconds, when the halving is repeated.

questions.question: The radius of an aluminium-27 nucleus is about
questions.explanation: R = 1.2 × 27^{1/3} = 1.2 × 3 = 3.6 fm. Cube roots of small integers (8 → 2, 27 → 3, 64 → 4) make these instant.

questions.question: A nucleus emits two alpha particles and one beta-minus particle. The changes in A and Z are
options: A decreases by 8 and Z decreases by 4
A decreases by 4 and Z decreases by 2
A is unchanged and Z increases by 1
A decreases by 8 and Z decreases by 3
questions.explanation: Each alpha takes away 4 from A and 2 from Z (total −8, −4); beta-minus converts a neutron into a proton, adding +1 to Z. Net: A − 8, Z − 3.

questions.question: The mean life τ of a radioactive substance is related to its half-life T½ by
questions.explanation: τ = 1/λ and T½ = 0.693/λ, so τ = T½/0.693 ≈ 1.44 T½. The mean life is always longer than the half-life.

questions.question: A radioactive sample of 80 g has a half-life of 5 years. The mass left after 15 years is
questions.explanation: 15 years is three half-lives: 80 → 40 → 20 → 10 g. This halving ladder is much faster than using the exponential formula.

questions.question: The ratio of the radii of two nuclei of mass numbers 8 and 64 is
questions.explanation: R ∝ A^{1/3}: cube roots are 2 and 4, giving 1 : 2. Mass numbers differ by a factor 8 but radii only by 2.

questions.question: In the fission of a uranium nucleus, about 200 MeV is released. This is mainly because
options: the fragments have higher binding energy per nucleon than the parent
questions.explanation: BE per nucleon rises from about 7.6 MeV (U) to about 8.4 MeV (fragments). The difference, multiplied by 236 nucleons, is the released energy.

questions.question: In an intrinsic semiconductor at room temperature,
options: the number of electrons equals the number of holes
questions.explanation: Every electron excited across the gap leaves behind a hole, so n_e = n_h. Adding impurity breaks this balance — that is what doping is for.

questions.question: Doping silicon with a pentavalent impurity such as phosphorus gives
options: an n-type semiconductor with electrons as majority carriers
a material with no free carriers
questions.explanation: Four of phosphorus's five valence electrons bond; the fifth is nearly free. Pentavalent → n-type (negative majority carriers), trivalent → p-type.

questions.question: The conductivity of a semiconductor
questions.explanation: Heat frees more electron–hole pairs, so σ rises — a NEGATIVE temperature coefficient, exactly opposite to a metal. This is why thermistors are made of semiconductors.

questions.question: In a p-n junction under forward bias,
options: the depletion region narrows and the barrier height decreases
questions.explanation: Forward bias pushes carriers towards the junction to neutralise part of the space charge: the barrier (0.7 V for Si) is overcome and current flows easily.

questions.question: The output ripple frequency of a full-wave rectifier fed with 50 Hz AC is
questions.explanation: A full-wave rectifier delivers one pulse per half cycle, so the ripple is 2f = 100 Hz. A half-wave rectifier gives only 50 Hz.

questions.question: A Zener diode used as a voltage regulator is operated
questions.explanation: Below the knee voltage it is an ordinary diode; when forward biased it behaves as a normal diode. Therefore Zener diodes are always operated in reverse bias.

questions.question: For a transistor to work as an amplifier, its emitter-base junction and collector-base junction must be
options: forward biased and reverse biased respectively
questions.explanation: The forward-biased emitter injects carriers; the reverse-biased collector sweeps them out. Reversing the two biases would put the transistor in saturation or cut-off.

questions.question: Which gate is called the universal gate?
questions.explanation: Any logic circuit can be built using NAND gates alone — combinations of NAND give NOT, AND, OR, NOR. NOR is the other universal gate.

questions.question: The output of a two-input AND gate with inputs A = 1, B = 0 is
questions.explanation: AND gives 1 only when ALL inputs are 1. With B = 0 the output is 0, whatever A is.

questions.question: The output of a NAND gate with both inputs at logic 1 is
questions.explanation: NAND = NOT of AND. AND(1, 1) = 1, so NAND(1, 1) = 0. This single case is why NAND is the basic building block of digital circuits.

questions.question: A transistor has β = 100 and base current 20 μA. The collector and emitter currents are
questions.explanation: I_C = βI_B = 100 × 20 μA = 2 mA; I_E = I_B + I_C = 2.02 mA. The emitter current is always the largest of the three.

questions.question: If α = 0.98 for a transistor, its β is
questions.explanation: β = α/(1 − α) = 0.98/0.02 = 49. A small α change causes a large β change because of the division by (1 − α).

questions.question: The barrier potential of a silicon diode and a germanium diode are approximately
questions.explanation: Si ≈ 0.7 V, Ge ≈ 0.3 V. Germanium diodes are used where a smaller forward drop matters, silicon where thermal stability matters.

questions.question: In a common-emitter amplifier, the phase difference between the input and output signals is
questions.explanation: Increasing the base current increases the collector current and hence the drop across the load resistor, lowering the output voltage: hence 180° inversion.

questions.question: A photodiode is operated in reverse bias because
options: it emits light in reverse bias
the fractional change in minority-carrier current with illumination is easier to measure
questions.explanation: In reverse bias, the reverse saturation current is produced by minority carriers, which illumination dramatically increases. The LED is the opposite device, used in forward bias.

questions.question: The energy band gap of an insulator is typically
questions.explanation: Insulators (diamond ≈ 5.5 eV) cannot have electrons excited across the gap at room temperature. Semiconductors sit near 1 eV, conductors have overlapping bands.
